chapters.title: Chapter 1111
paragraphs: Boom, boom, ba-boom!
There was nothing strange about hearing a war drum in the middle of a battle.
The drum on the highest watchtower was practically another command post, keeping watch over the walls on all sides.
But its beat had never sounded so urgent, so perilous. Something in it gripped the hearts of everyone who heard it.
*Slice!*
A streak of light shot across the foot of the wall like a bolt of lightning.
Dozens of fanatics charging in while scattering Sword Energy were cut to pieces and sent flying. Yet the man responsible for this display of divine might wore a rigid expression.
“This is...”

His words trailed off. The Slaughter Saint, who had been fighting enemies right beneath the wall, turned on instinct—not toward the Inner City, where the drum was sounding, but toward the west, where a muffled roar reached him from far away.
Even he didn’t know exactly why.
All he knew was that his instincts, honed by countless experiences, and the immense surge of power that had boiled over from the west moments ago were stirring every one of his senses.
For an instant, even the streaks of light plunging down from above slipped from his mind.
*Shreeeeeeek!*
Countless ice spikes rained down, freezing the air around them.
The Slaughter Saint felt the chill bearing down on him, but he didn’t take his eyes off the west.
Someone he could trust stood behind him.
*Whoosh!*
The wall lit up. A beam of light shot from someone’s fingertips and swallowed hundreds of ice spikes whole.
*KABOOOOOM!*
A blinding flash erupted with a thunderous crash.
Before the shockwaves of the collision had fully faded, the Bow Saint’s clear Sound Transmission rang in the Slaughter Saint’s ears.
—The West Gate has fallen.
The Slaughter Saint swallowed the groan rising in his throat.

The ominous premonition he’d feared had come true. But that left him even less time to lament. With one of the pillars holding their already fragile balance now completely broken, everything was in danger.
—Then the allies defending the West Gate...
—More than half are casualties, according to the numbers confirmed so far. They say the Embroidered Uniform Guard bought us at least a little time by fighting to the death.
Half.
It was no wonder the Slaughter Saint bit his lip at that staggering number.
More than ten thousand defenders had been stationed at the West Gate. And half of them had vanished—in barely half an hour after the battle began in earnest.
—What happened to the survivors?
—Some retreated to the Inner City. Others seem to still be holding off the enemy from the rear.
—Then, could it be...
A grim thought crossed his mind, and he fell silent. The Bow Saint’s quiet Sound Transmission continued.
—Cheongpung and Jin Taekyung. The two of them retreated to the Inner City.
—...They were lucky.
The Slaughter Saint held back a sigh of relief.
After so many had already been lost, it wouldn’t be right to focus only on the survival of those two just because he had ties to them.
But the Bow Saint had more to tell him.
—If those two are alive, we still have a chance. While they defend the Inner City, we can strike back as hard as—
—Even that won’t be easy. Not in their current condition.
—What... do you mean?
—Jin Taekyung is badly injured, I’m told. Cheongpung isn’t in good shape, either.
The Slaughter Saint’s eyes widened.
He stopped moving without realizing it. A blade swung at his shoulder.
*Slice!*
The strike was fast and powerful. He twisted aside at the last moment, but the Sword Energy carried by the blade grazed him and cut his skin.
Of course, even the man lucky enough to land that remarkable hit couldn’t escape death.
*Thud!*
A dagger flew from the Slaughter Saint’s fingertips and buried itself between the enemy’s brows. At the same time, his figure blurred like a ghost and shot up the wall.
*Whoosh, slice!*
In the blink of an eye, he stood atop the wall, cutting down enemies climbing by chains and ladders as his lips moved.
—How bad?
The Bow Saint kept firing arrows of Force at the enemy as she answered.
—They can’t say whether he’ll live.
—...Blood Lord. We underestimated that bastard.
A low groan escaped the Slaughter Saint.
He hadn’t been comfortable leaving the West Gate to Jin Taekyung from the start. He’d only been persuaded by the same argument they had used with Jeok Cheongang.
—We shouldn’t have left him there after all.
—It wouldn’t have changed anything, as long as the Blood Lord’s intentions stayed the same.
—I have to go to the Inner City. Hold this gate until then.
There was no time to waste.
If Jin Taekyung’s life hung by a thread, the Slaughter Saint was the only one who could pull him back from death.
With a heavy heart, he turned to leave.
Or tried to.
Until a clear voice reached his ears.
“Is that really the best choice?”
“...What do you mean?”
“Without you, Slaughter Saint, we can’t hold this gate. I certainly can’t hold it alone.”
The Slaughter Saint had no answer.
Of course he knew how dangerous their position was here, at the South Gate.
Even apart from the Grand Sorceress, they faced four Black Ghosts. The mages supporting them were still hurling spells at the wall while granting the fanatics greater strength and speed.
That was why he’d been forced to leave his assigned post at the East Gate and join the defense of the South Gate after only fifteen minutes.
But...
“Are you saying we should just let him—Jin Taekyung—die?”
The Bow Saint met his disbelieving gaze. When she spoke, her voice was graver than he had ever heard it.
“We may have no choice. If that is the death fate has given him.”
“That boy needs the Divine Physician. I know. But right now, all of us need the Slaughter Saint.”
“So which choice is best?”
The Slaughter Saint’s eyelids trembled.
Her question pierced his heart like an awl, and he knew the answer better than anyone.
Yet the woman standing before him felt like a stranger.
*Why?*
He knew why the Bow Saint had reappeared after vanishing for so long. He’d heard how she had followed a letter left by the Martial God, spending years searching for the one called the “chosen one.”
That made her words and actions now all the harder to understand.
Why wasn’t she trying to save the chosen one—or rather, Jin Taekyung?
There was something in her eyes and voice that he couldn’t begin to fathom. It was more than simple faith that Taekyung would survive.
*Bow Saint, what exactly are you hiding?*
He forced down the question on the tip of his tongue, along with the doubts racing through his mind.
The enemy’s assault was growing fiercer, as though it would not allow him even a moment to think.
*Fwoooosh.*
A massive sphere of flame suddenly turned the sky red, blotting out the wind and rain.
It hurtled toward them with terrifying force. The Slaughter Saint leaped from the wall to meet it without hesitation.
*Whoosh!*
A streak of light cut through the air along the path traced by his fingertips. A rift opened, followed by an explosion.
*KABOOOOOM!*
The ball of fire shattered into hundreds of pieces and scattered in every direction. The Slaughter Saint landed where he had started and fixed a profound gaze on the Bow Saint.
“Is that answer enough?”
Perhaps she saw the change in his eyes. A bitter smile crossed her lips.
“It does.”
Leaving her behind, the Slaughter Saint silently turned to face the enemies, who had dyed the land outside the wall pitch-black.
More precisely, he looked toward the one who had just displayed magic of a power beyond anything they’d seen so far.
*The Grand Sorceress.*
The face of another ringleader, who had finally stepped forward, burned itself onto the Slaughter Saint’s eyes. Four Black Ghosts stood around her like guards.
Then—
*Rumble...*
A chilling vibration rose from deep beneath the earth. The Slaughter Saint turned his head in one direction.
He thought of the one person who cherished Jin Taekyung more than anyone in the world—the one person who would rush into any danger for him.
*You’re the only one left now. I’m counting on you, Fire King.*
Just as the Slaughter Saint murmured those words in his heart—
*Rrrrrumble!*
The ground within a radius of roughly a hundred jang around the South Gate heaved its vast, heavy body upward.
A man’s voice rang out across the battlefield.
“Shake it.”
Earthquake.
*KABOOOOOM!*
*Rumble!*
The violent tremor began in the south and spread in every direction. Those who felt it reacted in different ways.
“A-an earthquake!”
Some thought of a disaster no human strength could stop and were seized by fear.
“Don’t falter! What is there left to fear?”
Others, already prepared to die, fought the enemy without giving an inch.
“Damn bitch. She hasn’t noticed already, has she?”
And one man, recognizing the power, fired blood-red flashes at the moths foolish enough to block his path to the Inner City.
He needed to take one man’s life quickly—and for good—before anything else could get in his way.
But that man—the Blood Lord—didn’t know what was happening several hundred jang away at the North Gate.
A massacre far beyond anything he had expected.
“A-a demon...”
*Cough.*
Blood mixed with bits of entrails spilled from the old monk’s lips.
His bright yellow robe was soaked through, its original color nowhere to be seen. Blackened corpses lay scattered in every direction.
None of them knew how many people had met such a terrible end.
Not even the man who had created this hellscape.
There was only one thing he knew for certain.
*Crack.*
The middle-aged monk whose neck he had just broken in his grasp was the last survivor of the Twelve Secret Monks, renowned as Tibet’s finest.
“Now you’re the only one left.”
The old monk standing rigid as a statue was the only obstacle still in his way.
The Dalai Lama’s eyes were wide open, his pupils trembling.
Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King, took a weary step toward him.
He thought of his Disciple, who must be in danger by now.
He reminded himself of his resolve.
“Let’s finish this quickly. He’s waiting.”
*Fwoosh.*
A white flame spread across his fatigue-dimmed pupils.

There was nothing strange about hearing a war drum in the middle of a battle.
The drum on the highest watchtower was practically another command post, keeping watch over the walls on all sides.

A streak of light shot across the foot of the wall like a bolt of lightning.
Dozens of fanatics charging in while scattering Sword Energy were cut to pieces and sent flying.

His words trailed off.

The Slaughter Saint, who had been fighting enemies right beneath the wall, turned on instinct—not toward the Inner City, where the drum was sounding, but toward the west, where a muffled roar reached him from far away.
Even he didn’t know exactly why.
All he knew was that his instincts, honed by countless experiences, and the immense surge of power that had boiled over from the west moments ago were stirring every one of his senses.
For an instant, even the streaks of light plunging down from above slipped from his mind.
*Shreeeeeeek!*
Countless ice spikes rained down, freezing the air around them.
The Slaughter Saint felt the chill bearing down on him, but he didn’t take his eyes off the west.
Someone he could trust stood behind him.
*Whoosh!*
The wall lit up.
A beam of light shot from someone’s fingertips and swallowed hundreds of ice spikes whole.
*KABOOOOOM!*
A blinding flash erupted with a thunderous crash.
Before the shockwaves of the collision had fully faded, the Bow Saint’s clear Sound Transmission rang in the Slaughter Saint’s ears.
—The West Gate has fallen.
The Slaughter Saint swallowed the groan rising in his throat.
The ominous premonition he’d feared had come true.
But that left him even less time to lament.
With one of the pillars holding their already fragile balance now completely broken, everything was in danger.
—Then the allies defending the West Gate...
—More than half are casualties, according to the numbers confirmed so far.
They say the Embroidered Uniform Guard bought us at least a little time by fighting to the death.
Half.
It was no wonder the Slaughter Saint bit his lip at that staggering number.
More than ten thousand defenders had been stationed at the West Gate.
And half of them had vanished—in barely half an hour after the battle began in earnest.
—What happened to the survivors?
—Some retreated to the Inner City.
Others seem to still be holding off the enemy from the rear.
—Then, could it be...
A grim thought crossed his mind, and he fell silent.
The Bow Saint’s quiet Sound Transmission continued.
—Cheongpung and Jin Taekyung.
The two of them retreated to the Inner City.
—...They were lucky.
The Slaughter Saint held back a sigh of relief.
After so many had already been lost, it wouldn’t be right to focus only on the survival of those two just because he had ties to them.
But the Bow Saint had more to tell him.
—If those two are alive, we still have a chance.
While they defend the Inner City, we can strike back as hard as—
—Even that won’t be easy.
Not in their current condition.
—What... do you mean?
—Jin Taekyung is badly injured, I’m told.
Cheongpung isn’t in good shape, either.
The Slaughter Saint’s eyes widened.
He stopped moving without realizing it.
A blade swung at his shoulder.
*Slice!*
The strike was fast and powerful.
He twisted aside at the last moment, but the Sword Energy carried by the blade grazed him and cut his skin.
Of course, even the man lucky enough to land that remarkable hit couldn’t escape death.
*Thud!*
A dagger flew from the Slaughter Saint’s fingertips and buried itself between the enemy’s brows.
At the same time, his figure blurred like a ghost and shot up the wall.
*Whoosh, slice!*
In the blink of an eye, he stood atop the wall, cutting down enemies climbing by chains and ladders as his lips moved.
—How bad?
The Bow Saint kept firing arrows of Force at the enemy as she answered.
—They can’t say whether he’ll live.
—...Blood Lord.
We underestimated that bastard.
A low groan escaped the Slaughter Saint.
He hadn’t been comfortable leaving the West Gate to Jin Taekyung from the start.
He’d only been persuaded by the same argument they had used with Jeok Cheongang.
—We shouldn’t have left him there after all.
—It wouldn’t have changed anything, as long as the Blood Lord’s intentions stayed the same.
—I have to go to the Inner City.
Hold this gate until then.
There was no time to waste.
If Jin Taekyung’s life hung by a thread, the Slaughter Saint was the only one who could pull him back from death.
With a heavy heart, he turned to leave.
Or tried to.
Until a clear voice reached his ears.
“Is that really the best choice?”
“...What do you mean?”
“Without you, Slaughter Saint, we can’t hold this gate.
I certainly can’t hold it alone.”
The Slaughter Saint had no answer.
Of course he knew how dangerous their position was here, at the South Gate.

paragraphs: *Is this a dream?*
The Dalai Lama wondered.
At the same time, he wished more desperately than ever that it was. If this was all a terrible nightmare, he wanted to wake from it as soon as possible—and never have another like it.
But—
*Grind.*
The pain in the lip he’d bitten without realizing it, the stench of blood in his nostrils, and the acrid smoke all around him whispered the same truth.
That this utterly horrific, unbelievable scene was real.
“Truly... a fiend if ever there was one.”
The Dalai Lama’s words came out like a groan.

The man reflected in the old monk’s eyes looked like a fiend torn from an ancient scripture. He had burned to death the Twelve Secret Monks—his Disciples and fellow martial brothers—and even the two Black Ghosts who had been such dependable reinforcements.
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang.”
His voice trembled with anger and fear.
The fiend striding toward him, by contrast, showed no hint of hesitation.
*Whoosh.*
Embers scattered. The air grew hot.
The Dalai Lama’s eyes flew wide as Jeok Cheongang closed more than ten jang in an instant and rushed straight at him, white flames flickering at his fingertips.
*BOOM!*
Compressed air exploded, and the flames swallowed wind and rain.
*KABOOOOOM!*
Was this what a wave of fire looked like?
Watching the searing heat sweep through the place where he had stood moments ago, the Dalai Lama felt a chill run down his spine.
“Flame Divine Palm...!”
There was no way he could mistake it.

It was the fiend’s martial art, recorded by his ancestors and passed down for more than two hundred years—the very technique that had sent all twelve Secret Monks, including two Supreme Peak masters, to their deaths.
“You recognize it? Did word of this old man reach all the way to that backwater?”
*Whoosh!*
Jeok Cheongang’s low voice sounded above him, accompanied by the rush of air. Emerging through the acrid smoke, he drove a tightly clenched fist down toward the crown of the Dalai Lama’s head.
The Flame-Extinguishing Divine Fist—the technique that had reduced the two Black Ghosts to ash before the Twelve Secret Monks met their end.
*KABOOM!*
The ground shook. A pillar of fire shot upward, and the rolling heat burned skin at a mere brush.
*Sizzle.*
It felt like a branding iron pressed to his flesh.
Yet the Dalai Lama dodged by a hair once more and thrust both palms forward with all his strength.
*Crack!*
Their hands met. The immense qi within them tangled and collided without pause.
But unlike a moment ago, the fear was gradually fading from the Dalai Lama’s eyes as he clashed head-on with Jeok Cheongang.
*He’s strong, but that’s all.*
He could feel it clearly through their joined hands. The qi of the man who had displayed such unbelievable power mere moments ago was wavering sharply.
It was the truth his fear had briefly hidden from him—and the truth Jeok Cheongang had wanted to conceal.
Nothing comes without a price.

Perfected Being Hyeoncheon of the Kongtong Sect, who had helped Jeok Cheongang defend the North Gate, was already down with severe internal injuries after a battle involving no fewer than five Supreme Peak masters.
Even Jeok Cheongang could not have come through it unscathed. Realizing this at last, the Dalai Lama fixed a cold gaze on the enemy before him. His anger, briefly driven back by fear, returned.
“You’re gravely mistaken.”
“What?”
“We didn’t learn of you through you, Fire King Jeok Cheongang. We learned of you through your predecessor—the one who should have fallen into the Eight Hot Hells long ago.”
The Dalai Lama bit off each syllable.
“Our Potala Palace never forgot. No—we came to a point where we could never forget.”
It had all begun more than two hundred years ago, on the day a wild-haired stranger in blood-red rags set foot in Tibet.
For the Potala Palace, it was the deepest, most devastating wound—and a history of humiliation that could never be washed away.
*Bring in that suspicious foreigner staying at an inn in Chamdo immediately. I will personally interrogate him to find out who he is, where he came from, and why he’s here.*
The Dalai Lama who gave that order could never have guessed what would follow.
The Potala Palace considered its influence in Tibet comparable to that of the Demonic Cult. Surely even an ignorant foreigner would not dare defy them.
Nor could he have imagined that the foreigner would leave the twenty-odd martial monks sent to capture him half-crippled, then storm the palace himself, eyes rolled back in his head.
*Who are you? Which bald bastard ordered you to smash the first meal this old man has seen in three days?*
Perhaps that had been their last chance.

They could have apologized for the martial monks’ rather rough attempt to approach him. They could have prepared enough meat and liquor to make the table sag, to make up for interrupting his long-awaited meal. Then, once the mood had warmed like an oven stuffed with firewood, they could have talked.
If only they had done that.
But as the records attest, events took no such heartwarming turn.

Twenty martial monks had already been left half-crippled for overturning his table and trying to use their weapons. And the Potala Palace, which strictly observed its principles of non-killing and abstinence, had neither liquor nor meat on hand to calm him.

When the furious stranger stormed into the main palace that day, he found no table sagging beneath meat and liquor. Instead, he found two hundred martial monks who could break a person’s limbs with their bare hands.
Among them were the Dalai Lama of that era, acknowledged by all as Tibet’s greatest master, and four of the Twelve Secret Monks who served at his side.
*You seem to be a fairly well-known martial artist from the Central Plains... Surrender peacefully now, and I’ll settle this with twenty years of wall-gazing meditation. What do you say, donor?*
The stranger’s answer was firm.
*That’s a terrible deal. I refuse.*
*Good grief. You’re making this difficult.*
*You bald monks made this what it is. This old man hasn’t done a damn thing wrong. At least, not yet.*
*...Not yet?*
*Ahem. Anyway, I was planning to rest for a while and leave quietly. This time, at least.*
*...This time, at least?*

*I didn’t like it when bald monks I’d never seen before came barging in out of nowhere. But if you’d waited quietly in a corner until I finished eating, I would’ve gone along with it. Hell, if you hadn’t tried to force me down, none of this would’ve happened.*
*I can’t say you’re entirely wrong. Still, even allowing for my Disciples’ slight discourtesy, your response was excessive.*
*They overturned my precious meal and even tried to use weapons. You call that a slight discourtesy?*
Faced with that pointed question, the Dalai Lama chose silence over admitting the truth. The stranger studied him—the man already seemed more martial artist than monk—and sighed deeply.
*Hearing you say that, I deeply regret it.*
*Oh? Truly?*
*Of course. I swear it to Heaven and Earth.*
The stranger’s next words sealed everyone’s fate.
*I should’ve crippled them completely instead of leaving them half-crippled.*
*...You’re a fiend to the bone. What can be done now? It’s come to this. Please, don’t hold it against us. May you find peace in your next life.*
And so, the killing began.
A storm of blood swept through, driven by one side alone.
A dreadful storm of blood that would be remembered for more than two hundred years, and would still be remembered a thousand years later, as long as the Potala Palace endured.
“One hundred died there that day. Another hundred were crippled.”
Recalling his sect’s humiliation, the Dalai Lama spoke in a harsh, grating voice. His gaze on Jeok Cheongang was colder than ever, and the anger in his steady voice had swallowed his fear.
“The Dalai Lama of that time died too.”
The four Twelve Secret Monks who had been there with him barely survived, but like the martial monks who lived through it, they were never able to use martial arts again.
“It was a terrible humiliation. Something that should never have happened—something we had thought impossible.”
All of it had taken barely half a day. The Potala Palace’s martial monks, scattered across Tibet to maintain order, rushed back to the main palace with all their might.
There, at last, they saw it.
The once-imposing palace lay in ruins. Scrawled across a charred pillar that had been wrenched from the ground was a single line:
The Jade Emperor says: Even a dog should be left alone while it eats.
Beneath that saying of highly dubious origin, the writer had carefully inscribed his credentials in a style every bit as long and grandiose.
“Fifth Sect Leader of the great Fire Gate Clan. Ghost Flame Fist Songhak.”
The Dalai Lama ground out the accursed name that had been passed down to this day.
“If we’d captured him then, none of this would be happening today.”
But the martial monks had not captured Ghost Flame Fist Songhak and sent him to meet Yama.
After branding the Potala Palace with an indelible humiliation, he had melted through the net over heaven and earth cast by Tibet’s Murim and headed straight for the Central Plains.

Before that, he had fled the Mad Wind Society of the great desert—the reason he had entered Tibet at all. Their pursuit had kept him from eating for three days, a particular hardship for the man who valued his meals more than any other Sect Leader in the Fire Gate Clan’s history.
Songhak returned to the clan’s home on Mount Jiuhua in high spirits and wrote a brief account of his thrilling exploits.

I have always held the Fourth Ancestor, the Third Sect Leader, in the deepest respect. Following in his footsteps, I traveled the world and the Outer Murim. As it happened, I fought the Mad Wind Society of the great desert beyond the scorching sands and uprooted the Potala Palace’s very pillars. At this, all the men and horses of Tibet grew enraged and pursued me. But who am I? I am Ghost Flame Fist Songhak, Fifth Sect Leader of the great Fire Gate Clan. Without so much as a hair harmed, I... avoided them and returned safely to the Central Plains.
Of course, Ghost Flame Fist Songhak had no idea that more than two hundred years later, a distant descendant would find this proud record and mutter that he was a madman.
Nor did he know the Potala Palace would nurse its grudge for so long.
In truth, he had not cared in the slightest.
“I learned later that before all that, he’d slaughtered more than five hundred of the Mad Wind Society’s mounted bandits in the desert.”
The Mad Wind Society had tried to steal Songhak’s horse and lost most of its leadership instead. Unable to recover from the damage, it eventually vanished into history.
The Potala Palace, however, did not.
With no rival in Tibetan Murim, its members quietly vowed revenge.
Some scholarly monks urged forgiveness and mercy to prevent further bloodshed, but their voices could not overcome the fury of the martial monks, who were closer to martial artists than to monks.
And so the Potala Palace gradually changed.
Its members began spending more time with martial arts manuals than with scriptures. They accepted only children with exceptional aptitude and greatly expanded their ranks of martial monks.
“We swore that even if Ghost Flame Fist died and turned to dust before we could avenge that day, we would end the line of those fiends with our own hands.”
By the time the land had changed nearly ten times over, the Potala Palace had grown into a fighting force far stronger than it had ever been. Even its members believed the time for revenge had come.
But the man who had been chosen as the new Dalai Lama in childhood, according to Potala Palace tradition, was not satisfied. That had been about a hundred years ago.
“We had grown stronger, certainly. But it was still nowhere near enough. To take our revenge ourselves, we would have to face the entire Central Plains.”

Just as Songhak had been shunned as a foreigner the moment he set foot in Tibet, the Potala Palace would be nothing but an outsider in the Central Plains. A dangerous outsider, at that—one with enough power to unleash a storm of bloodshed.

The Fire Gate Clan might have spent years stirring up trouble and accumulating gratitude and grudges, but the martial artists of the Central Plains would never seek out the Fire Gate Clan and hand it over to dangerous outsiders from the west for revenge.
“In the end, we needed greater strength. Or... an ally who would join us against the Central Plains.”
*Crack.*
The force in the Dalai Lama’s hands suddenly surged, pushing Jeok Cheongang’s hands back little by little.
The balance between them was finally breaking.
“The Demonic Cult was truly foolish. The arrogant Heavenly Demon mocked us for being weak. That was his greatest mistake.”
“The Great Faction War... Hah. I thought you were just a bald monk consumed by an old grudge with no claim to justice. Now I can’t even call you a monk.”
Jeok Cheongang forced down the blood rising in his throat and gave the Dalai Lama a scornful look.
“How ridiculous. Don’t you think?”
“What?”
“Look at yourself. You’ve joined hands with fiends worse than the Demonic Cult, and you dare call anyone else a fiend?”
The Dalai Lama flinched.
Jeok Cheongang’s sudden rebuke carried a terrifying aura. In the flames blazing within Jeok’s eyes, the Dalai Lama finally saw what he had become.
Red. His eyes were red.
Their light had taken on the color of the pool of blood at his feet.
Slowly, but steadily.
“All for that pathetic power, you even broke a taboo.”
His eyes and voice trembled.
But nothing he said could undo the truth of the past.
He had needed to grow stronger. Somehow, he had needed more and more power.
The countless pills and martial arts Dark Heaven offered had made that possible.
No—more precisely, that new power, infused with demonic energy, had made it possible.
Jeok Cheongang gave a quiet laugh. The Dalai Lama had been confronted with a contradiction he had forgotten—or had tried desperately to ignore.
“If you’ve got nothing to say, shut your mouth. Even this old man, with a strong stomach, can’t stand the excuses coming off a fiend’s tongue.”
“You bastard! Shut your mouth!”
*Fwoosh!*
A vast wave of energy surged in every direction.
Using his blazing rage as kindling, the Dalai Lama finally wrung every last bit of power and potential from deep within himself and drove his full strength against the enemy before him.
*Crack!*
The balance had tipped decisively. Bones shifted, and the flames around Jeok Cheongang’s hands began to dim.
Then, through lips streaked with blood—a testament to his mounting injuries and exhaustion—Jeok Cheongang released a single azure dragon’s roar.
“Hyeoncheon! Now!”
At that moment—
*Shhhhh.*
The world seemed to slow. The Dalai Lama tore his hands free of Jeok Cheongang’s with all his strength and spun around, every hair on his body standing on end.
He remembered the man who had slipped from his thoughts: the Kongtong Sect Leader, whom he had believed unable to fight.
Far away, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon was leaning against the corpse of a huge elephant, drawing only the faintest breaths. The Dalai Lama froze.
No.
*Crack!*
The terrible heat that drove deep into his body did not allow him even that instant.
His body shuddered as if lightning had pierced it.
Yet no blood spilled from him. Not a single scream escaped his lips. The flames had vaporized the blood that should have burst forth, and the pain was so overwhelming he forgot even to cry out.
But perhaps the worst pain of all was his enemy’s low voice, sounding beside his ear.
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang says: Never harm a being who has something it must protect, even if that being is a beast.”

Like the ancestor who had carved his own words into a Potala Palace pillar, Jeok Cheongang whispered in a faint but clear voice. His hand had pierced the Dalai Lama’s back and burst through his chest. He clenched it tight.
“Especially if that being belongs to the Fire Gate Clan.”
The Dalai Lama could not answer.
His senses cut off from the world, and darkness swallowed his sight.
“Go on ahead, fiend of Tibet. This old man still has something to protect.”
*Thud.*
At last, his head slumped.
With his enemy’s final words echoing like Yama’s, the Dalai Lama’s world closed around him.

sentences.text: *Is this a dream?*
The Dalai Lama wondered.
At the same time, he wished more desperately than ever that it was.
If this was all a terrible nightmare, he wanted to wake from it as soon as possible—and never have another like it.
But—
*Grind.*
The pain in the lip he’d bitten without realizing it, the stench of blood in his nostrils, and the acrid smoke all around him whispered the same truth.
That this utterly horrific, unbelievable scene was real.
“Truly... a fiend if ever there was one.”
The Dalai Lama’s words came out like a groan.
The man reflected in the old monk’s eyes looked like a fiend torn from an ancient scripture.
He had burned to death the Twelve Secret Monks—his Disciples and fellow martial brothers—and even the two Black Ghosts who had been such dependable reinforcements.
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang.”
His voice trembled with anger and fear.
The fiend striding toward him, by contrast, showed no hint of hesitation.
*Whoosh.*
Embers scattered.
The air grew hot.
The Dalai Lama’s eyes flew wide as Jeok Cheongang closed more than ten jang in an instant and rushed straight at him, white flames flickering at his fingertips.
*BOOM!*
Compressed air exploded, and the flames swallowed wind and rain.
*KABOOOOOM!*
Was this what a wave of fire looked like?
Watching the searing heat sweep through the place where he had stood moments ago, the Dalai Lama felt a chill run down his spine.
“Flame Divine Palm...!”
There was no way he could mistake it.

It was the fiend’s martial art, recorded by his ancestors and passed down for more than two hundred years—the very technique that had sent all twelve Secret Monks, including two Supreme Peak masters, to their deaths.
“You recognize it?
Did word of this old man reach all the way to that backwater?”
*Whoosh!*
Jeok Cheongang’s low voice sounded above him, accompanied by the rush of air.
Emerging through the acrid smoke, he drove a tightly clenched fist down toward the crown of the Dalai Lama’s head.
The Flame-Extinguishing Divine Fist—the technique that had reduced the two Black Ghosts to ash before the Twelve Secret Monks met their end.
*KABOOM!*
The ground shook.
A pillar of fire shot upward, and the rolling heat burned skin at a mere brush.
*Sizzle.*
It felt like a branding iron pressed to his flesh.
Yet the Dalai Lama dodged by a hair once more and thrust both palms forward with all his strength.
*Crack!*
Their hands met.
The immense qi within them tangled and collided without pause.
But unlike a moment ago, the fear was gradually fading from the Dalai Lama’s eyes as he clashed head-on with Jeok Cheongang.
*He’s strong, but that’s all.*
He could feel it clearly through their joined hands.
The qi of the man who had displayed such unbelievable power mere moments ago was wavering sharply.
It was the truth his fear had briefly hidden from him—and the truth Jeok Cheongang had wanted to conceal.
Nothing comes without a price.

Perfected Being Hyeoncheon of the Kongtong Sect, who had helped Jeok Cheongang defend the North Gate, was already down with severe internal injuries after a battle involving no fewer than five Supreme Peak masters.
Even Jeok Cheongang could not have come through it unscathed.
Realizing this at last, the Dalai Lama fixed a cold gaze on the enemy before him.
His anger, briefly driven back by fear, returned.
“You’re gravely mistaken.”
“What?”
“We didn’t learn of you through you, Fire King Jeok Cheongang.
We learned of you through your predecessor—the one who should have fallen into the Eight Hot Hells long ago.”
The Dalai Lama bit off each syllable.
“Our Potala Palace never forgot.
No—we came to a point where we could never forget.”
It had all begun more than two hundred years ago, on the day a wild-haired stranger in blood-red rags set foot in Tibet.
For the Potala Palace, it was the deepest, most devastating wound—and a history of humiliation that could never be washed away.
*Bring in that suspicious foreigner staying at an inn in Chamdo immediately.
I will personally interrogate him to find out who he is, where he came from, and why he’s here.*
The Dalai Lama who gave that order could never have guessed what would follow.
The Potala Palace considered its influence in Tibet comparable to that of the Demonic Cult.
Surely even an ignorant foreigner would not dare defy them.
Nor could he have imagined that the foreigner would leave the twenty-odd martial monks sent to capture him half-crippled, then storm the palace himself, eyes rolled back in his head.
*Who are you?
Which bald bastard ordered you to smash the first meal this old man has seen in three days?*
Perhaps that had been their last chance.
They could have apologized for the martial monks’ rather rough attempt to approach him.
They could have prepared enough meat and liquor to make the table sag, to make up for interrupting his long-awaited meal.
Then, once the mood had warmed like an oven stuffed with firewood, they could have talked.
If only they had done that.
But as the records attest, events took no such heartwarming turn.
Twenty martial monks had already been left half-crippled for overturning his table and trying to use their weapons.
And the Potala Palace, which strictly observed its principles of non-killing and abstinence, had neither liquor nor meat on hand to calm him.
When the furious stranger stormed into the main palace that day, he found no table sagging beneath meat and liquor.
Instead, he found two hundred martial monks who could break a person’s limbs with their bare hands.
Among them were the Dalai Lama of that era, acknowledged by all as Tibet’s greatest master, and four of the Twelve Secret Monks who served at his side.
*You seem to be a fairly well-known martial artist from the Central Plains...
Surrender peacefully now, and I’ll settle this with twenty years of wall-gazing meditation.
What do you say, donor?*
The stranger’s answer was firm.
*That’s a terrible deal.
I refuse.*
*Good grief.
You’re making this difficult.*
*You bald monks made this what it is.
This old man hasn’t done a damn thing wrong.
At least, not yet.*
*...Not yet?*
*Ahem.
Anyway, I was planning to rest for a while and leave quietly.
This time, at least.*
*...This time, at least?*
*I didn’t like it when bald monks I’d never seen before came barging in out of nowhere.
But if you’d waited quietly in a corner until I finished eating, I would’ve gone along with it.
Hell, if you hadn’t tried to force me down, none of this would’ve happened.*
*I can’t say you’re entirely wrong.
Still, even allowing for my Disciples’ slight discourtesy, your response was excessive.*
*They overturned my precious meal and even tried to use weapons.
You call that a slight discourtesy?*
Faced with that pointed question, the Dalai Lama chose silence over admitting the truth.
The stranger studied him—the man already seemed more martial artist than monk—and sighed deeply.
*Hearing you say that, I deeply regret it.*
*Oh?
Truly?*
*Of course.
I swear it to Heaven and Earth.*
The stranger’s next words sealed everyone’s fate.
*I should’ve crippled them completely instead of leaving them half-crippled.*
*...You’re a fiend to the bone.
What can be done now?
It’s come to this.
Please, don’t hold it against us.
May you find peace in your next life.*
And so, the killing began.
A storm of blood swept through, driven by one side alone.
A dreadful storm of blood that would be remembered for more than two hundred years, and would still be remembered a thousand years later, as long as the Potala Palace endured.
“One hundred died there that day.
Another hundred were crippled.”
Recalling his sect’s humiliation, the Dalai Lama spoke in a harsh, grating voice.
His gaze on Jeok Cheongang was colder than ever, and the anger in his steady voice had swallowed his fear.
“The Dalai Lama of that time died too.”
The four Twelve Secret Monks who had been there with him barely survived, but like the martial monks who lived through it, they were never able to use martial arts again.
“It was a terrible humiliation.
Something that should never have happened—something we had thought impossible.”
All of it had taken barely half a day.
The Potala Palace’s martial monks, scattered across Tibet to maintain order, rushed back to the main palace with all their might.
There, at last, they saw it.
The once-imposing palace lay in ruins.
Scrawled across a charred pillar that had been wrenched from the ground was a single line:
The Jade Emperor says: Even a dog should be left alone while it eats.
Beneath that saying of highly dubious origin, the writer had carefully inscribed his credentials in a style every bit as long and grandiose.
“Fifth Sect Leader of the great Fire Gate Clan.
Ghost Flame Fist Songhak.”
The Dalai Lama ground out the accursed name that had been passed down to this day.
“If we’d captured him then, none of this would be happening today.”
But the martial monks had not captured Ghost Flame Fist Songhak and sent him to meet Yama.
After branding the Potala Palace with an indelible humiliation, he had melted through the net over heaven and earth cast by Tibet’s Murim and headed straight for the Central Plains.
Before that, he had fled the Mad Wind Society of the great desert—the reason he had entered Tibet at all.
Their pursuit had kept him from eating for three days, a particular hardship for the man who valued his meals more than any other Sect Leader in the Fire Gate Clan’s history.
Songhak returned to the clan’s home on Mount Jiuhua in high spirits and wrote a brief account of his thrilling exploits.
I have always held the Fourth Ancestor, the Third Sect Leader, in the deepest respect.
Following in his footsteps, I traveled the world and the Outer Murim.
As it happened, I fought the Mad Wind Society of the great desert beyond the scorching sands and uprooted the Potala Palace’s very pillars.
At this, all the men and horses of Tibet grew enraged and pursued me.
But who am I?
I am Ghost Flame Fist Songhak, Fifth Sect Leader of the great Fire Gate Clan.
Without so much as a hair harmed, I... avoided them and returned safely to the Central Plains.
Of course, Ghost Flame Fist Songhak had no idea that more than two hundred years later, a distant descendant would find this proud record and mutter that he was a madman.
Nor did he know the Potala Palace would nurse its grudge for so long.
In truth, he had not cared in the slightest.
“I learned later that before all that, he’d slaughtered more than five hundred of the Mad Wind Society’s mounted bandits in the desert.”
The Mad Wind Society had tried to steal Songhak’s horse and lost most of its leadership instead.
Unable to recover from the damage, it eventually vanished into history.
The Potala Palace, however, did not.
With no rival in Tibetan Murim, its members quietly vowed revenge.
Some scholarly monks urged forgiveness and mercy to prevent further bloodshed, but their voices could not overcome the fury of the martial monks, who were closer to martial artists than to monks.
And so the Potala Palace gradually changed.
Its members began spending more time with martial arts manuals than with scriptures.
They accepted only children with exceptional aptitude and greatly expanded their ranks of martial monks.
“We swore that even if Ghost Flame Fist died and turned to dust before we could avenge that day, we would end the line of those fiends with our own hands.”
By the time the land had changed nearly ten times over, the Potala Palace had grown into a fighting force far stronger than it had ever been.
Even its members believed the time for revenge had come.
But the man who had been chosen as the new Dalai Lama in childhood, according to Potala Palace tradition, was not satisfied.
That had been about a hundred years ago.
“We had grown stronger, certainly.
But it was still nowhere near enough.
To take our revenge ourselves, we would have to face the entire Central Plains.”
Just as Songhak had been shunned as a foreigner the moment he set foot in Tibet, the Potala Palace would be nothing but an outsider in the Central Plains.
A dangerous outsider, at that—one with enough power to unleash a storm of bloodshed.

The Fire Gate Clan might have spent years stirring up trouble and accumulating gratitude and grudges, but the martial artists of the Central Plains would never seek out the Fire Gate Clan and hand it over to dangerous outsiders from the west for revenge.
“In the end, we needed greater strength.
Or... an ally who would join us against the Central Plains.”
*Crack.*
The force in the Dalai Lama’s hands suddenly surged, pushing Jeok Cheongang’s hands back little by little.
The balance between them was finally breaking.
“The Demonic Cult was truly foolish.
The arrogant Heavenly Demon mocked us for being weak.
That was his greatest mistake.”
“The Great Faction War...
Hah.
I thought you were just a bald monk consumed by an old grudge with no claim to justice.
Now I can’t even call you a monk.”
Jeok Cheongang forced down the blood rising in his throat and gave the Dalai Lama a scornful look.
“How ridiculous.
Don’t you think?”
“What?”
“Look at yourself.
You’ve joined hands with fiends worse than the Demonic Cult, and you dare call anyone else a fiend?”
The Dalai Lama flinched.
Jeok Cheongang’s sudden rebuke carried a terrifying aura.
In the flames blazing within Jeok’s eyes, the Dalai Lama finally saw what he had become.
Red.
His eyes were red.
Their light had taken on the color of the pool of blood at his feet.
Slowly, but steadily.
“All for that pathetic power, you even broke a taboo.”
“N-no.
His eyes and voice trembled.
But nothing he said could undo the truth of the past.
He had needed to grow stronger.
Somehow, he had needed more and more power.
The countless pills and martial arts Dark Heaven offered had made that possible.
No—more precisely, that new power, infused with demonic energy, had made it possible.
Jeok Cheongang gave a quiet laugh.
The Dalai Lama had been confronted with a contradiction he had forgotten—or had tried desperately to ignore.
“If you’ve got nothing to say, shut your mouth.
Even this old man, with a strong stomach, can’t stand the excuses coming off a fiend’s tongue.”
“You bastard!
Shut your mouth!”
*Fwoosh!*
A vast wave of energy surged in every direction.
Using his blazing rage as kindling, the Dalai Lama finally wrung every last bit of power and potential from deep within himself and drove his full strength against the enemy before him.
*Crack!*
The balance had tipped decisively.
Bones shifted, and the flames around Jeok Cheongang’s hands began to dim.
Then, through lips streaked with blood—a testament to his mounting injuries and exhaustion—Jeok Cheongang released a single azure dragon’s roar.
“Hyeoncheon!
Now!”
At that moment—
*Shhhhh.*
The world seemed to slow.
The Dalai Lama tore his hands free of Jeok Cheongang’s with all his strength and spun around, every hair on his body standing on end.
He remembered the man who had slipped from his thoughts: the Kongtong Sect Leader, whom he had believed unable to fight.
Far away, Perfected Being Hyeoncheon was leaning against the corpse of a huge elephant, drawing only the faintest breaths.
The Dalai Lama froze.
No.
*Crack!*
The terrible heat that drove deep into his body did not allow him even that instant.
His body shuddered as if lightning had pierced it.
Yet no blood spilled from him.
Not a single scream escaped his lips.
The flames had vaporized the blood that should have burst forth, and the pain was so overwhelming he forgot even to cry out.
But perhaps the worst pain of all was his enemy’s low voice, sounding beside his ear.
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang says: Never harm a being who has something it must protect, even if that being is a beast.”
Like the ancestor who had carved his own words into a Potala Palace pillar, Jeok Cheongang whispered in a faint but clear voice.
His hand had pierced the Dalai Lama’s back and burst through his chest.
He clenched it tight.
“Especially if that being belongs to the Fire Gate Clan.”
The Dalai Lama could not answer.
His senses cut off from the world, and darkness swallowed his sight.
“Go on ahead, fiend of Tibet.
This old man still has something to protect.”
*Thud.*
At last, his head slumped.
With his enemy’s final words echoing like Yama’s, the Dalai Lama’s world closed around him.

chapters.title: Chapter 1113
paragraphs: Nothing can be gained without sacrifice.
That was even more true for those seeking victory through war—the most terrible form of violence—in an age of savagery that had thrown law and benevolence to the dogs.
But even knowing that cruel reality, there were some things one could never get used to.
Like realizing that someone who had been laughing and talking with you not long ago was gone.
“...So, that’s how it ended.”
After hearing what had happened immediately after he lost consciousness, Jin Taekyung quietly closed his eyes, muttering to himself.
Faces came to mind. So many people who, though he had known them only a short time, had looked at him with trust.
Along with them came the stony face and voice of someone whose presence had gradually become familiar.
“It doesn’t matter who you are. The Embroidered Uniform Guard obeys only His Majesty the Emperor’s command. If you stand in our way in defiance of his imperial decree, I’ll kill you.”
“Perhaps it’s because you’re a martial artist without even an identity tag, but your manners are atrocious.”
“Thank you. For protecting us—for protecting the imperial family.”
Fleeting moments brushed faintly past his eyes and ears.
And at the end of those memories was always the figure of someone who had pressed forward without wavering.
“Jeong Hogun, Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, answers the command of the Marquis of Shangshan!”
Remembering the voice he would never hear again, Taekyung opened his eyes without a word and forced down something rising from deep in his chest.
The officer had been so stubbornly steadfast it was almost foolish. He had always been calm, and always stood tall.
Taekyung had lost consciousness before witnessing Jeong Hogun’s final moments, but he was certain the man had faced them the same way.
Because that was who he was.
The Embroidered Uniform Guards who had served under Taekyung over the past three months must have been the same. So must the defenders at the West Gate, who had fought with their lives on the line.
They had all fought to protect others and died valiantly.
Taekyung would never forget that their sacrifice had allowed so many people, himself included, to survive.
Neither would the person beside him, head bowed and shedding tears.
“...I’m sorry, Benefactor. I wasn’t good enough.”
Cheongpung’s eyes glistened, and his voice trembled.
Looking at Cheongpung as he blamed himself, Jin Taekyung spoke in a calm voice.
“You’re right. We weren’t good enough. Neither you nor I.”
“No. You did everything you could. If only I’d been a little stronger...”
“Young Hero Cheongpung.”
“Yes?”
“If only the Blood Lord—no, the Lord of Heaven—had never been born. That would’ve been nice, wouldn’t it?”
“If, maybe, what if... Get those stupid thoughts out of your head. Even if you’re sorry to the dead, even if you hate yourself like crazy for surviving, bear it.”
*Grit.*

Jin Taekyung slowly shifted his body, which had been propped against the Inner City wall. He clenched his jaw without meaning to, against the terrible pain that seemed to reach every cell in his body.
So were the fury and self-reproach he had been struggling to hold back since regaining consciousness. No matter how hard he suppressed them, they kept surging up from deep in his chest.
His legs suddenly went slack like a puppet with its strings cut.
He caught the wall but staggered, and Cheongpung hurriedly reached out to support him.
Or tried to.
Before Cheongpung’s hand could touch him, Taekyung firmly shook his head.
“B-Benefactor.”
Cheongpung watched, his eyes wavering, as Taekyung forced himself upright. Beads of sweat ran down Taekyung’s forehead, and his face was deathly pale.
But what showed on the outside was not the whole story.
Cheongpung had poured his own internal energy into Taekyung to lend him strength. He knew better than anyone that the damage inside his body was even worse than it looked.
Some of the tears he had shed earlier had come from a terrible premonition: that he would be unable to stop Jin Taekyung from dying.
But—
Thump.
Taekyung did not stop. He did not give up.
Bearing the pain with everything he had and suppressing the emotions boiling like lava in his chest, he gripped the wall and stood again.
Slowly. Stubbornly.
Each second felt like ten years as he forced the words out.
“Think about why we survived. Why they had to give their lives to save us.”
They could not fall apart. They must not.
If they gave up now, it would all have been for nothing.
The sacrifice of those who had died opening a path of retreat.
The sacrifice of others who might be dying even now.
“Apologize to the dead and cry your eyes out after we’ve finished everything we have to do.”
He wasn’t speaking only to Cheongpung.
Jin Taekyung kept speaking resolutely to everyone around him. Their heads hung low, their faces marked by desperation or defeat. Exhausted in body and mind, they had briefly forgotten their duty.
“That’s the only way... we can show them the respect they deserve. It’s our duty.”
*Step.*
Taekyung finally took a step after forcing out those last words.
The air around them thrummed. An unseen surge rose together with a wave of heat.
One step.
He had taken only one step.
He was a pitiful sight, a young man so covered in blood that no one would have been surprised if he collapsed on the spot.
Yet simply watching him made their hearts pound.
The heavy sense of defeat that had gripped them began to lift, and something hot filled the space it left behind.
*Thump. Thump. Thump.*
A pulse began to spread like ripples across a still pond. No one knew who had started it, or where.
Outside the Inner City, the war drums beat faster and faster, announcing the approach of death. But that did not matter.

Not now. Not while they stood with him—a martial artist who had made his way through a mountain of sabers and a forest of swords, a marquis of the Great Nation, and, beyond that, a fellow subject living in this vast realm.
For a moment, they could forget.
And remember what they had forgotten.
*KABOOM!*
Even when a thunderous crash sounded in the distance and the war drums that had seemed destined to ring forever fell silent.
*Rumble-rumble-rumble!*
Countless enemies came sweeping down the avenue toward the Inner City, their footsteps shaking the ground.
*Clang-clang-clang!*
Steel rang out, and desperate screams filled the air.
*Thump-thump-thump-thump!*
Still, the defenders stamped their feet with all their strength and struck their weapons against the ground, coaxing the embers of their battle cry back into flame.
They thought of the countless people huddled deep inside the Inner City, trembling.
Their eyes, alight with renewed fire, fixed on one man.
“Remember this, all of you.”
His voice had grown clear. They watched the silver-white spearhead rise slowly.
“Remember what we’ve stayed alive for.”
*Shing.*
He spat out the words, and the spearhead gave off a frost-sharp aura.
*Whoosh.*
Behind him, standing tall as an iron tower, strands of violet light rose and blazed brighter than torches, illuminating the darkness.
And beneath the energy of the Zaha Divine Technique spreading like the sunset at dusk, the corner of one person’s eye was no longer wet.
His voice, sunk deeper than ever, was the same.
“I’ll do it. I promise.”
The battle was not over yet.
Red. Everything was red.
At least, everything one man could see was awash in corpses and blood.
*Slice!*
How many lives vanished in the space of a single deep breath?
Heads flew here and there. Limbs were severed. Some people died slowly in agony.
They had once been Daoists in fluttering white robes, as refined as immortals; soldiers fed by the nation they served; martial artists and common people. Now it was impossible to tell them apart.
Covered in blood from head to toe, they had become part of the hellscape painted across Xining’s main road.
The man who had drawn its first stroke—and would put the final mark on it—watched the slaughter unfold before him.
*What fools.*
He couldn’t understand it.
What were they fighting for?
An Emperor whose bloodline alone had qualified him to rule?
Or that embarrassing notion they called “justice,” which did not even have a form?
*Ridiculous.*

Most of them had probably never seen the Emperor’s face. And the justice the martial artists of the Central Plains would die for was nothing more than something they had made up within their own little circle.
But the Lord of Heaven was different. He alone was different.
His power and overwhelming presence made the Blood Lord tremble simply by being near him.
In a world where might made right, what ruler could be more fitting?
*This loyal servant will fulfill your wish.*
The Blood Lord shot forward with a vow he could not tell whether he was making to the Lord of Heaven or to himself.
*Whoosh!*
A chillingly low whistle cut through the air. A moment later, the front line of defenders blocking the road to the Inner City crumpled, though they had not given up the fight.
A hundred bodies fell like puppets with their strings cut. Fountains of dark blood shot high above them.
*Splatter!*
Blood rained in every direction.
Among the defenders who witnessed the unbelievable sight, a trembling voice spoke.
“A-a monster...”
“Yes. I suppose that’s what I look like to you.”
The Blood Lord smiled and reached out.
*BOOM!*
A flash of blood-red light swelled and exploded. The blast swallowed the screams, scattering torn flesh and bone.
“But after he takes the world, who will call me a monster?”
It was a world where might made right.
The day was not far off when a blood-mad monster would be hailed as a divine general sent by Heaven.
Though he had failed to take the life of one man whose death was necessary for that great undertaking—
“Open the way, you worthless moths.”
*Slice! Stab-stab-stab!*
To the Blood Lord, it was all only a matter of time.
The Inner City was close enough to see now. As long as fierce fighting continued at the other three walls, no one could stand in his way.
*Grand Sorceress, you bitch, stay out of this. Even I don’t want to kill a servant girl the Lord of Heaven favors with my own hands.*
The Blood Lord was about to resume the slaughter when—
*Whoosh! BOOM!*
A sharp, dazzling flash blocked the steps of the monster who had seemed impossible to stop.

Some of the tears he had shed earlier had come from a terrible premonition: that he would be unable to stop Jin Taekyung from dying.
But—
Thump.
Taekyung did not stop.
He did not give up.
Bearing the pain with everything he had and suppressing the emotions boiling like lava in his chest, he gripped the wall and stood again.
Slowly.
Stubbornly.
Each second felt like ten years as he forced the words out.
“Think about why we survived.
Why they had to give their lives to save us.”
They could not fall apart.
They must not.
If they gave up now, it would all have been for nothing.
The sacrifice of those who had died opening a path of retreat.
The sacrifice of others who might be dying even now.
“Apologize to the dead and cry your eyes out after we’ve finished everything we have to do.”
He wasn’t speaking only to Cheongpung.
Jin Taekyung kept speaking resolutely to everyone around him.
Their heads hung low, their faces marked by desperation or defeat.
Exhausted in body and mind, they had briefly forgotten their duty.
“That’s the only way... we can show them the respect they deserve.
It’s our duty.”
*Step.*
Taekyung finally took a step after forcing out those last words.
The air around them thrummed.
An unseen surge rose together with a wave of heat.
One step.
He had taken only one step.
He was a pitiful sight, a young man so covered in blood that no one would have been surprised if he collapsed on the spot.
Yet simply watching him made their hearts pound.
The heavy sense of defeat that had gripped them began to lift, and something hot filled the space it left behind.
*Thump.
Thump.
Thump.*
A pulse began to spread like ripples across a still pond.
No one knew who had started it, or where.
Outside the Inner City, the war drums beat faster and faster, announcing the approach of death.
But that did not matter.
Not now.

Not while they stood with him—a martial artist who had made his way through a mountain of sabers and a forest of swords, a marquis of the Great Nation, and, beyond that, a fellow subject living in this vast realm.
For a moment, they could forget.
And remember what they had forgotten.
*KABOOM!*
Even when a thunderous crash sounded in the distance and the war drums that had seemed destined to ring forever fell silent.
*Rumble-rumble-rumble!*
Countless enemies came sweeping down the avenue toward the Inner City, their footsteps shaking the ground.
*Clang-clang-clang!*
Steel rang out, and desperate screams filled the air.
*Thump-thump-thump-thump!*
Still, the defenders stamped their feet with all their strength and struck their weapons against the ground, coaxing the embers of their battle cry back into flame.
They thought of the countless people huddled deep inside the Inner City, trembling.
Their eyes, alight with renewed fire, fixed on one man.
“Remember this, all of you.”
His voice had grown clear.
They watched the silver-white spearhead rise slowly.
“Remember what we’ve stayed alive for.”
*Shing.*
He spat out the words, and the spearhead gave off a frost-sharp aura.
*Whoosh.*
Behind him, standing tall as an iron tower, strands of violet light rose and blazed brighter than torches, illuminating the darkness.
And beneath the energy of the Zaha Divine Technique spreading like the sunset at dusk, the corner of one person’s eye was no longer wet.
His voice, sunk deeper than ever, was the same.
“I’ll do it.
I promise.”
The battle was not over yet.
Red.
Everything was red.
At least, everything one man could see was awash in corpses and blood.
*Slice!*
How many lives vanished in the space of a single deep breath?
Heads flew here and there.
Limbs were severed.
Some people died slowly in agony.
They had once been Daoists in fluttering white robes, as refined as immortals; soldiers fed by the nation they served; martial artists and common people.
Now it was impossible to tell them apart.
Covered in blood from head to toe, they had become part of the hellscape painted across Xining’s main road.
The man who had drawn its first stroke—and would put the final mark on it—watched the slaughter unfold before him.
*What fools.*
He couldn’t understand it.
What were they fighting for?
An Emperor whose bloodline alone had qualified him to rule?
Or that embarrassing notion they called “justice,” which did not even have a form?
*Ridiculous.*
Most of them had probably never seen the Emperor’s face.
And the justice the martial artists of the Central Plains would die for was nothing more than something they had made up within their own little circle.
But the Lord of Heaven was different.
He alone was different.
His power and overwhelming presence made the Blood Lord tremble simply by being near him.
In a world where might made right, what ruler could be more fitting?
*This loyal servant will fulfill your wish.*
The Blood Lord shot forward with a vow he could not tell whether he was making to the Lord of Heaven or to himself.
*Whoosh!*
A chillingly low whistle cut through the air.
A moment later, the front line of defenders blocking the road to the Inner City crumpled, though they had not given up the fight.
A hundred bodies fell like puppets with their strings cut.
Fountains of dark blood shot high above them.
*Splatter!*
Blood rained in every direction.
Among the defenders who witnessed the unbelievable sight, a trembling voice spoke.
“A-a monster...”
“Yes.
I suppose that’s what I look like to you.”
The Blood Lord smiled and reached out.
*BOOM!*
A flash of blood-red light swelled and exploded.
The blast swallowed the screams, scattering torn flesh and bone.
“But after he takes the world, who will call me a monster?”
It was a world where might made right.
The day was not far off when a blood-mad monster would be hailed as a divine general sent by Heaven.
Though he had failed to take the life of one man whose death was necessary for that great undertaking—
“Open the way, you worthless moths.”
*Slice!
Stab-stab-stab!*
To the Blood Lord, it was all only a matter of time.
The Inner City was close enough to see now.
As long as fierce fighting continued at the other three walls, no one could stand in his way.
*Grand Sorceress, you bitch, stay out of this.
Even I don’t want to kill a servant girl the Lord of Heaven favors with my own hands.*
The Blood Lord was about to resume the slaughter when—
*Whoosh!
BOOM!*
A sharp, dazzling flash blocked the steps of the monster who had seemed impossible to stop.

paragraphs: The beam of light that crossed the space between them in an instant was dazzling—and devastating.
Even barehanded, the Blood Lord had been slaughtering the defenders without mercy. Now the flash forced him to draw the beloved blade that had rested quietly at his waist.
*BOOM!*
A deafening crash—and blood sprayed in every direction.
But this time, it wasn’t the defenders’ blood. It belonged to the fanatics who followed him.
“C-cough. Blood Lord...”
Was the man lucky or unlucky?

Dozens of his comrades had been caught in the sudden flash and died without even a chance to scream. He had barely survived. He crawled toward the Blood Lord, hoping the great Apostle chosen by the Lord of Heaven would ease his pain, even a little.
And the Blood Lord answered his desperate plea.
With the weight of a thousand geun behind his foot.
*Crunch!*
The man’s spine shattered. That was the end of it.
The Blood Lord didn’t know whether the man had been grasping at the last thread of life or hoping for the peace of death.
No, that wasn’t quite right. The death of a nobody, little more than a disposable pawn, had never interested him in the first place.
His gaze had been fixed all along beyond the thick cloud of dust.
“Come out.”
The instant his cold voice left his lips—
*Whoosh!*
A flash burst from the dust and hurtled toward him.
More precisely, it was heat that shone like a flash of light.
*Fwoosh—BOOM!*
Flames swept through the air.
Their terrible heat turned suspicion into certainty. The Blood Lord brought the Red Blade down with all his might.
*Slice!*
The flames split to either side with a sharp cutting sound.
The avenue, more than twenty jang wide, was engulfed in fire. Through the rising heat haze, a figure wavered.
“Where are you in such a hurry to go?”
The voice was low and steady.
Even through the heat haze, the eyes pouring out flames shone clearly.
Fire King Jeok Cheongang.
The Blood Lord’s eyes narrowed at the sight of him. He hadn’t expected Jeok to appear yet. Perhaps he had thought he would never see him again.
“So the head of the Ten Kings, whom the orthodox faction praises so highly, is just another warrior after all. You abandoned all those allies to save your one and only disciple?”
Certain Jeok had deserted the North Gate to come here, the Blood Lord spoke with scorn.
Jeok Cheongang caught his breath before replying. “I never asked anyone to praise me. But there’s a reason for everything.”
“What?”
“Ever since the day I defeated a thousand demonic soldiers, the world has called me the Fire King. It’s been so long I was starting to tire of the name... Perhaps that will change after today.”
The Blood Lord’s face twisted as he finally understood what Jeok’s arrival meant.

The Potala Palace forces sent to the North Gate had been formidable. There was the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s greatest master, and the Twelve Secret Monks, who included two Supreme Peak masters, greenhorns though they were.
Two Black Ghosts had been sent as well, in case anything unexpected happened. They should have been capable of more than holding Jeok in place. It wouldn’t have been surprising if they’d killed him.
*But how?*
The Blood Lord had no answer to the question that sprang to mind. Perhaps he never would.
The battle between those fighting to protect something and those consumed entirely by revenge could often defy expectations by a wide margin.
And Fire King Jeok Cheongang had someone he would protect even at the cost of everything he had.
“Did you think a few bald monks like that could stop this old man?”
The Blood Lord clenched his teeth at the low voice.
“You crazy old bastard. No matter how hard you struggle, nothing will change.”
“I have protected him. And I will protect him.”
“That precious disciple of yours? The one who might be dying right now?”
“...What did you say?”
Jeok Cheongang faltered. The Blood Lord’s mouth twisted into a smile.
“No. Perhaps he’s already dead. Last I saw him, he was at death’s door.”
“You dare...!”
The news of his disciple’s danger shook Jeok more than he could hide.
*Whoosh!*
With a faint whistle of air, the Blood Lord vanished like a phantom. He crossed more than ten jang and struck.
*Slice!*
The ground split like tofu.
Jeok Cheongang twisted aside just in time to avoid the blow, but blood spurted from several places on his body.
*Drip, drip, drip!*
The force of the blade was enough to wound him without touching him.
Jeok knew better than anyone what that blood scattering through the air meant.
*My body...!*
It felt as heavy as a thousand geun. Even his senses were slow to respond.
In his anger and desperation, he had forgotten how exhausted the battle at the North Gate had left him—and how badly a moment’s emotional turmoil could cost him in a life-and-death duel.
The Blood Lord saw it, too.
*BOOM!*
Blade strikes tore through the air like a storm.
Dozens—no, hundreds—of attacks poured back and forth, as though slicing time itself apart. Already exhausted, Jeok Cheongang sensed that this fight was close to its end.
He knew that end would be his death. He also knew he had one move left that might change it.
*Dance of the Fire God and Demon.*
A final flame fueled by everything he had.
The divine art had been passed down through generations of the Fire Gate Clan, yet its terrible aftermath had made it forbidden. Jeok Cheongang had nearly died from using it once already.
But now it was all he had left. It was the only way to defeat the Blood Lord, whose power came closer to Regeneration than mere healing.
Even that brief moment of thought might have been more than Jeok could afford.
*An opening!*
The Blood Lord’s eyes flashed.
*Whoom!*
The Red Blade was buried deep in the ground. Instead, he drove a fist toward Jeok’s side like a cannonball, putting all his strength behind it.
For some reason, his strength and speed had grown greater still since Jin Taekyung’s One Annihilation had put him in danger.
Jeok had no time even to gasp.
His body was exhausted, his senses dulled, and his internal energy was nearly spent. All he could do was cross his Force-clad arms and brace with everything he had.
*BOOM!*
His vision overturned.
The blow hurled Jeok more than ten jang through the air and straight through a large inn that had once been crowded with people.
*CRASH!*
A pillar collapsed. Splinters flew.
Not until he had smashed through seven buildings, beginning with the inn, did Jeok cough up the hot surge rising from his gut.
*Splatter.*
Blackened blood stained an alley he didn’t recognize.
Through his blurring vision, he saw the Blood Lord rushing toward him like a gale. Joy and killing intent burned together in those blood-red eyes.
“Jeok Cheongang!”
The Blood Lord roared his name and brought the Red Blade down.
*CLANG!*
A sharp crash rang out.
The Blood Lord was forced back, eyes wide with disbelief, after deflecting five streaks of light fired from an unexpected angle.
*Whoooom.*
A vibration ran through his grip.
The Red Blade trembled, then steadied. The Blood Lord’s face, twisted like a Fiend’s, did not.
“Not bad... But after living this long, you ought to know when to stay out of a fight. Don’t you think?”
He slowly turned his head as he growled.
His blood-red gaze fell on the five old men standing between him and Jeok Cheongang.
“If you don’t want to be torn limb from limb and die.”
Despite the killing intent bearing down on them, the slender old Daoist at their center quietly helped Jeok to his feet.
*Fwoosh.*
Internal energy flowed into Jeok, and a little color returned to his deathly pale face. He coughed up another mouthful of blood.
“Thank you for all your hard work,” the old Daoist said calmly. “We’ll take it from here.”
“Cough. You’re...”
“Jin Taekyung may not have much time left.”
“Go. Quickly. It’s for everyone’s sake, too.”
Of course, the old Daoist’s “everyone” left out one person.
“Ha. Now there are six crazy old men.”
Sneering, the Blood Lord angled the Red Blade downward.
“Then you can all die.”
*Whoosh!*
A crescent of blood-red Force shot along the Red Blade. The Force alone was a full jang across, and the strike carried terrifying power.
The next instant—
*BOOM!*
A crash like the sky splitting apart rang out. Everything within a ten-jang radius crumbled to dust.
Above it stood six figures, high in the air.
The Blood Lord’s gaze darkened. The slender old Daoist bowed his head slightly to Jeok Cheongang, whom he had been supporting.
“Please forgive the impertinence of one so far your junior.”
Jeok was too drained to answer. Severe exhaustion and Internal Injury had been building since the North Gate.
No—there wasn’t even time for an answer. Before he could speak, the old Daoist’s arms swung with force.
“You crazy—!”
The Blood Lord’s frantic shout came too late.
*Whoooosh!*
Jeok Cheongang shot through the air toward the Inner City.
Before the enraged Blood Lord could pursue him, the five old Daoists landed softly on the ground and blocked his way.
They had the bearing of immortals, an aura like noble cranes, and a movement technique astonishing enough to match.
Only then did the Blood Lord recognize the intruders.
“The Kunlun Five Immortals.”
“You know us?”
“How could I not? I’ve heard the heartbreaking tale of five old men who should have died long ago, still eating up the Kunlun Sect’s rice.”
Naturally, the Blood Lord’s account bore little resemblance to their reputation.
The Kunlun Five Immortals were Martial Uncles to Cheongheoja, the current Sect Leader, and Elders who still upheld the Kunlun Sect well into their eighties.
Each had stopped just short of Supreme Peak. But they had grown up as close as brothers, and their combined technique was said to withstand even a Supreme Peak master.
To the Blood Lord, they were merely five more troublesome old moths.
“Get out of my sight. I’d tear you apart right now, but even that would waste time.”
The slender old Daoist, the eldest of the Kunlun Five Immortals, Perfected One Taecheong, shook his head.
“I cannot accept that offer. So I’d like to suggest an alternative.”
“There is no alternative. You’ve just thrown away your last chance.”
The Blood Lord let the Red Blade hang at an angle and stepped toward them.
First Jin Taekyung. Now Jeok Cheongang. Twice he had lost prey he’d nearly caught—prey he had to kill.

Their auras felt far stronger than their reputations suggested. That was puzzling, but even a combined technique capable of facing a Supreme Peak master would be a tower built on sand before him. It would fall in moments.
Or so he’d thought.
“You’re mistaken,” the old Daoist said. “We still have a chance.”
“What?”
“This is the alternative we came up with.”
Only then did the Blood Lord notice the calm smile on Perfected One Taecheong’s lips. Something was wrong.
*Shaaaaa.*
Power surged from Perfected One Taecheong—no, from all five of the Kunlun Five Immortals—and shook the air around them.
Their fierce aura was hard to believe in men whose skill was said to have stopped at the very edge of Peak. It was so rough, it made the immortal meaning of their title seem absurd.
It took the Blood Lord little time to recognize what felt so familiar about it.
“You... Don’t tell me.”
“It’s as fearsome as I heard, this Temporary Strength Pill.”
“No need to look so surprised. None of us has ever practiced demonic martial arts. We had to pay a price to take it.”
Perfected One Taecheong was telling the truth.
The Temporary Strength Pill’s power was chiefly for practitioners of demonic, heterodox arts—particularly those whose martial arts remained incomplete because they had not reached Supreme Peak.
Even if someone who cultivated pure qi took one of the spare pills carried by Dark Heaven’s followers, it would have little effect.
Unless they did something mad: broke the innate qi they had built up over more than eighty years and forced themselves to absorb the pill’s energy.
“To stop a monster...”
*Whoooom.*
His words faded beneath a deep rumble.
An unstable, hazy Force gathered around the sword in Perfected One Taecheong’s hand. There was no mistaking what it was.
And it wasn’t his sword alone. Force rose from the blades of all five Kunlun Five Immortals.
“If that’s what it takes, then we’ll gladly become monsters, too.”
*Whoosh!*
Space split, and six figures clashed in a tangle.
Fifteen minutes.
That was all the time the Kunlun Five Immortals remained on their feet.
But for someone else, they had bought a full fifteen minutes.
Perhaps that was why Perfected One Taecheong could smile even through the overwhelming pain as both his legs were torn off.
*Slice!*
Then his arms were severed.
*Boom!*
Even as the organs inside him tore apart, he swallowed his screams.
And when the shadow of death finally fell over him, the old Daoist held fast to his principles and offered a last farewell to his Junior Brothers, whose breathing had already ceased.
“Remember... Our deaths will not be in vain...”
*Crack!*
His brain matter burst out with a horrible pop.
The Blood Lord lifted his foot from Perfected One Taecheong’s shattered head.
“No. This is a meaningless death.”
As he slowly raised his head, cries sounded from every direction, louder and closer than before.
No. It was a creed of exactly eight characters.
Above heaven and below heaven, ten thousand demons bow in homage.
Above heaven and below heaven, let all things kneel.
“...So it shall be.”
Leaving those low words behind, the monster continued toward the Inner City.
Sticky blood followed in his wake.
