The slender old Daoist, the eldest of the Kunlun Five Immortals, Perfected One Taecheong, shook his head.
“I cannot accept that offer.
So I’d like to suggest an alternative.”
“There is no alternative.
You’ve just thrown away your last chance.”
The Blood Lord let the Red Blade hang at an angle and stepped toward them.
First Jin Taekyung.
Now Jeok Cheongang.
Twice he had lost prey he’d nearly caught—prey he had to kill.
Their auras felt far stronger than their reputations suggested.
That was puzzling, but even a combined technique capable of facing a Supreme Peak master would be a tower built on sand before him.
It would fall in moments.
Or so he’d thought.
“You’re mistaken,” the old Daoist said.
“We still have a chance.”
“What?”
“This is the alternative we came up with.”
Only then did the Blood Lord notice the calm smile on Perfected One Taecheong’s lips.
Something was wrong.
*Shaaaaa.*
Power surged from Perfected One Taecheong—no, from all five of the Kunlun Five Immortals—and shook the air around them.
Their fierce aura was hard to believe in men whose skill was said to have stopped at the very edge of Peak.
It was so rough, it made the immortal meaning of their title seem absurd.
It took the Blood Lord little time to recognize what felt so familiar about it.
“You...
Don’t tell me.”
“It’s as fearsome as I heard, this Temporary Strength Pill.”
“No need to look so surprised.
None of us has ever practiced demonic martial arts.
We had to pay a price to take it.”
Perfected One Taecheong was telling the truth.
The Temporary Strength Pill’s power was chiefly for practitioners of demonic, heterodox arts—particularly those whose martial arts remained incomplete because they had not reached Supreme Peak.
Even if someone who cultivated pure qi took one of the spare pills carried by Dark Heaven’s followers, it would have little effect.
Unless they did something mad: broke the innate qi they had built up over more than eighty years and forced themselves to absorb the pill’s energy.
“To stop a monster...”
*Whoooom.*
His words faded beneath a deep rumble.
An unstable, hazy Force gathered around the sword in Perfected One Taecheong’s hand.
There was no mistaking what it was.
And it wasn’t his sword alone.
Force rose from the blades of all five Kunlun Five Immortals.
“If that’s what it takes, then we’ll gladly become monsters, too.”
*Whoosh!*
Space split, and six figures clashed in a tangle.
Fifteen minutes.
That was all the time the Kunlun Five Immortals remained on their feet.
But for someone else, they had bought a full fifteen minutes.
Perhaps that was why Perfected One Taecheong could smile even through the overwhelming pain as both his legs were torn off.
*Slice!*
Then his arms were severed.
*Boom!*
Even as the organs inside him tore apart, he swallowed his screams.
And when the shadow of death finally fell over him, the old Daoist held fast to his principles and offered a last farewell to his Junior Brothers, whose breathing had already ceased.
“Remember...
Our deaths will not be in vain...”
*Crack!*
His brain matter burst out with a horrible pop.
The Blood Lord lifted his foot from Perfected One Taecheong’s shattered head.
“No.
This is a meaningless death.”
As he slowly raised his head, cries sounded from every direction, louder and closer than before.
No.
It was a creed of exactly eight characters.
Above heaven and below heaven, ten thousand demons bow in homage.
Above heaven and below heaven, let all things kneel.
“...So it shall be.”
Leaving those low words behind, the monster continued toward the Inner City.
Sticky blood followed in his wake.

chapters.title: Chapter 1115
paragraphs: It was a fierce battle.
Unprecedented in a thousand years of Murim history, stretching back to the day a monk from a distant land crossed the Yangtze on a single reed leaf.
It was a bloodbath, too.
One without precedent in the history of the entire continent, not just Murim.
*CRUNCH!*
A skull split open. Brain matter sprayed.
The boy died without so much as a final cry.
But no one grieved anymore for a boy soldier who hadn’t even reached twenty.
No—they couldn’t.
In the relentless turning of this brutal hellscape, death had long since become cheap.
The only thing they could do for the dead was take revenge.
“The Lord of Heaven is with us...!”
A bloodshot fanatic trampled the boy’s corpse as he stepped onto the wall.
*Thud.*
A gleaming blade burst out between his brows.
“Who’s with you?”
The fanatic, already dead, couldn’t answer.
A small shadow pulled the dagger from the back of his head as the body crumpled like a rotten log. Then the shadow stepped toward the other enemies, still elated at having seized the wall.
*Whoosh.*
The figure vanished like a ghost.
The Sword Energy that came flying a beat too late shot toward the space where the shadow had stood, but a cool breeze from somewhere had already swept past them.
*Slice—SPLAT!*
A fountain of blood arced into the pitch-black night sky.
The speed was blinding, every movement precise and free of waste. Yet after cutting down dozens of enemies in the blink of an eye, the shadow—the Slaughter Saint—looked grim.
*This is the limit. We can’t hold out any longer.*
He wasn’t thinking only of himself.
The South Gate had been an impregnable fortress with the Slaughter Saint and the Bow Saint defending it. Now the gate was faltering, along with every defender stationed there.
*It’s a miracle we held out this long.*
Perhaps the fight had been impossible from the start.
Their side had even needed to call up commoners, while the enemy were all trained in a certain level of martial arts and had used Temporary Strength Pills as well.
Outmatched in both numbers and quality, they had held on only by making the most of their defensive position and deploying their handful of elite troops wherever they were needed.
But—
*So this is as far as we go.*
The Slaughter Saint swallowed a groan and looked around.
Beyond the unrelenting downpour lay a sea of corpses and blood. His allies were collapsing from exhaustion, their bodies pushed far past the limits of their will.
Everyone was tired.
Their limbs felt as heavy as waterlogged cotton. Keeping their minds from giving way was all they could manage.
Even the Slaughter Saint felt his exhaustion mounting and his dantian running empty.
*If only we’d taken out the Grand Sorceress. We might have had a chance to counterattack...*
But the Grand Sorceress was no easy opponent. She was even more formidable than he’d heard.

The defenses around her and the hundred or so other mages had been as solid as an iron wall. When the Slaughter Saint threw everything he had into breaking through to its center, he found no fewer than four Black Ghosts waiting for him.
All four had been strengthened by an array of enhancement spells.
Without help from the greatest archer under Heaven, who could tear a target apart from hundreds of jang away, even the Slaughter Saint would not have returned with all his limbs intact.
Still, he had brought down two Black Ghosts. Pride and sheer determination had seen to that.
*Shing!*
A brilliant flash shattered his brief reverie.
*BOOM!*
A massive beam of light swallowed the twenty or so fanatics charging at him from behind and exploded.
“You seem relaxed. You even have time to look away.”
At the Bow Saint’s pointed remark, the Slaughter Saint flicked his sleeve.
*Thud-thud-thud!*
Enemies aiming their bows from blind spots crumpled all at once, each with a long, slender ox-hair needle embedded between the brows.
“I wish I looked relaxed. Maybe then those bastards would be a little scared.”
“Do you think they have any fear left?”
“...Damn it.”
The Slaughter Saint launched himself forward again with a bitter curse, trying to protect as many of his allies as he could from fiends who had mortgaged their very souls to fanatic faith.
*Slice! CRACK!*
He cut and stabbed, broke bones and twisted limbs.
But that was all he could do.

No matter how tirelessly the two giants who had once shone so brightly in their age cut down their enemies, the exhausted defenders’ resistance faded fast. The fanatics’ fervent voices filled the wall.
“Great Lord of Heaven!”
“Let your majesty and power descend upon this land!”
*Grit.*
Facing them felt like standing before an enormous wave. The Slaughter Saint clenched his teeth without realizing it.
Kill hundreds, and thousands followed. Cut down thousands, and tens of thousands stood behind them.
Would this battle ever end?
*What the hell are we supposed to do...?*
He couldn’t even finish the thought.
He was a man of flesh and blood, not an all-knowing, all-powerful god.
*...This is the first time I’ve wanted to see someone this badly.*
Was it the wounds scattered across his body? Or the internal energy draining away even now?

Caught in the exhaustion and emptiness he’d forgotten, the Slaughter Saint suddenly thought of someone who, long ago, had always brought him confidence and certain victory—even when facing a Demonic Cult army more than ten times their size.
*Martial God, what would you have done?*
It was a foolish question.
The Martial God would never have entertained such doubts in the first place. That was the kind of man he was.
A true heaven, beyond the reach of even the three brightest stars in all Murim.
And yet, at that moment, another name came to the Slaughter Saint.
*Jin Taekyung.*
The master of the Morning Star, the new star Dharma King Hong Dao had once spoken of—and now the young man who had drawn the Lord of Heaven’s inexplicable obsession.
And—
*The Chosen One.*
The Slaughter Saint could be sure of nothing.
Was it all coincidence? Or had someone high above, in the distant heavens, decided their fate long ago?
All he could do was hold tight to their one hope, even if it amounted to no more than a handful.
*Slice!*
Force streamed from his dagger as it cut through the air, bending like a whip to sweep across the wall.
Amid severed limbs and spilling blood, the Slaughter Saint drew on what little internal energy he had left and slaughtered the enemies before him in a single attack. Then he opened his mouth.
“Everyone, retreat.”
The defenders, barely managing to resist, stared at him wide-eyed. But he had made up his mind. His voice did not waver.

“Messenger, take word to the South and North Gates immediately. The elites stationed at each gate will cover the rear and buy us some time. The rest of the troops are to retreat as quickly and orderly as possible.”
Silence pressed down on them. It lasted only an instant, but felt like an eternity.
To them, abandoning the wall meant that the word they’d been trying so hard to ignore—defeat—was finally becoming real.
Only one person present could oppose the Slaughter Saint’s decision. The Bow Saint watched him, her gaze still calm.
*Is that the best we can do, then?*
Her Sound Transmission reached his ear.
The Slaughter Saint met her gaze and answered just as calmly.
*I don’t know. But... I want to believe.*
That was all.

He wanted to believe in the one person chosen by Dharma King Hong Dao, who had read the heavenly patterns; by the Blood Lord, who had thrown even those patterns into disarray; and by the Martial God, whose life or death was now unknown.
*I want to see with my own eyes where coincidence ends and fate begins.*
Even if a wretched end awaited him, he would not regret it.
The young brat he had watched as Mungyeong, not as the Slaughter Saint, had the makings of a Great Master worth risking his life for, regardless of age or martial prowess.
Surely they all felt the same.
*Bow Saint.*
At his quiet call, he looked steadily at her.
*I don’t know exactly what you have in mind. But there’s one thing I do know. No—anyone who’s been even a little close to Jin Taekyung knows it.*
*You can keep your distance and refuse to say a word, but you can’t bring yourself to hate that boy.*
*I want to believe in him. And in you, too.*
Her pupils wavered for an instant.
But neither her agitation nor her silence lasted long.
*Fwoosh!*
High above them, enormous balls of fire came pouring down like a meteor shower, evaporating even the driving rain.
*Shing!*
The Bow Saint’s hand moved like lightning. A dazzling arrow of light shot forth.
*KABOOM!*
A crash that seemed to split heaven and earth rang out, and the sky turned red.
The fireballs broke into hundreds, then thousands of pieces, large and small, and rained down. The Bow Saint watched them fall, her face set.
“Honestly, I don’t know what choice I should make.”
The Slaughter Saint was about to groan when she added quietly, “Still, I want to believe, too.”
“Come with me. To the Inner City. To that boy.”
At last, a faint smile touched the Slaughter Saint’s tired lips.

chapters.title: Chapter 1116
paragraphs: Xining Fortress, the last line of defense in Qinghai, was well suited to withstanding a siege.
But in the dozens of battles fought over the years, its high, sturdy walls had not been the only thing to give invaders nightmares.
“As expected, even those Fiends are having trouble crossing the moat.”
At the middle-aged Daoist’s admiring murmur, Cheongheoja, Sect Leader of the Kunlun Sect, nodded.
“Without it, this fight would be twice as hard. The gate would have fallen long ago.”
Even now, the moat—which was more than ten jang wide and quite deep—was forcing the enemy to pay a terrible price.

And crossing it was only the beginning. Beyond it waited a gate made of immensely thick black iron. No matter how skilled Dark Heaven’s fanatics were in martial arts, they had little choice but to suffer the losses and scale the walls instead.

The walls had been in danger at times, thanks perhaps to the enemy’s overwhelming numbers and the strength granted by their Temporary Strength Pills. But here at the East Gate, the defense was holding more easily than anywhere else.
If they could keep it that way, they might even win.
The middle-aged Daoist beside Cheongheoja seemed to share that hope.
“If we win this battle, we can all return to the main sect together, can’t we?”
“All of us together... How wonderful that would be.”
Cheongheoja’s voice was heavier than ever. The middle-aged Daoist’s expression turned bitter.
“Are you thinking about your second Disciple?”
Cheongheoja was silent for a moment, then shook his head.
“No.”
“Then...”
“I was thinking about the shortcomings of a foolish master who failed to guide his Disciple down the right path.”
“It was my fault. From beginning to end. All of it.”
“Master...”
The middle-aged Daoist—Cheongheoja’s Senior Disciple, Hak Su—looked at him with sorrow.
“Don’t blame yourself. It wasn’t your fault.”
“Is that what you think?”
“I know it. Everyone in Kunlun does. You kept your second Disciple closer than anyone else and took special care of him.”
“I had to. You were always gentle, and your third Junior Brother was full of energy. But that child always seemed rough and unsettled.”
“Wasn’t that why you gave him the Daoist name Hak Eui?”
“Yes. That was why.”

The boy who had grown up in dark, dangerous back alleys had gained a new name and a family. Cheongheoja had always urged his rough-tempered second Disciple to live up to that name and become a more righteous man.
To never forget, even for an instant, that he was a Daoist.
“But... who could have guessed he was a spy conspiring with Dark Heaven?”
Hak Su pressed his lips together and shook his head.
“I still can’t believe it. I don’t want to.”
His gaze shifted to the empty space beside him, as though his second Junior Brother might be standing there with his usual crooked look.
But that would never happen.
No. It was impossible.
Hak Eui was already dead.
Before dawn, he had resisted those who came under cover of night to capture the spy. In the end, he had lost his life.
Hak Su had arrived at the scene too late. He’d seen his master holding his Junior Brother’s severed head and a sword dripping with blood.
He’d seen his master with eyes sadder than ever—just like now.
“Master...”
Just as Hak Su looked at Cheongheoja, torn by conflicting thoughts—
*Whoosh!*
A sharp whistle cut through the air. A messenger came racing toward them, using his movement technique with all his might.
“Sect Leader!”
He was covered in blood, and his face was as white as a sheet.
Cheongheoja swallowed the groan that almost escaped him and spoke in a heavy voice.
“Where have you come from?”
“The South Gate. Hah... The South Gate.”
“Then the two Seniors have ordered a retreat to the Inner City?”
“How did you...?”
“I understand. It must be much the same elsewhere.”
No further words were needed. The messenger’s appearance had told Cheongheoja enough. He went on calmly.
“Go and tell them I’ll lead the East Gate forces to the Inner City shortly.”
“May fortune favor you in battle.”
The messenger bowed briefly and left. Hak Su’s face hardened.
“Go ahead without me. I’ll stay with some of the troops and buy you time.”
His eyes and voice were full of resolve, but Cheongheoja shook his head at once.
“I can’t leave you behind.”
Hearing the concern in his master’s voice, Hak Su gave a faint smile.
“The road to the Inner City won’t be easy. It may be even more dangerous than staying here. They need you more than they need me.”
It was a reasonable prediction.
The dire news that the West Gate had fallen to the Blood Lord had reached the East Gate just before the war drums were about to be destroyed.

Unlike the East Gate, where the enemy forces were comparatively weaker than at the other three gates, a retreat without a plan might lead them straight into the Blood Lord and his fanatics, who could be rampaging unchecked through the fortress from the West Gate.
Even so, Cheongheoja would not yield.
“I forbid it.”
“Master, we’re out of time!”
Hak Su could no longer contain his urgency. But then—
“Who is out of time?”
Cheongheoja’s voice sank strangely low, piercing Hak Su’s ear.
“Master...?”
“I asked who was out of time.”
Hak Su blinked at him, bewildered.
The old Daoist’s presence had changed so suddenly that the Kunlun Disciples who knew him well—and all the soldiers nearby—were staring at Cheongheoja.
Then an unexpected voice rang through the rain.
“Why hesitate? Your master, lofty as the heavens, has asked you a question.”
*Splash.*
A foot came down in a puddle, accompanied by a hard-edged voice.
At the same time, a man who looked to be around thirty took off his low-pulled straw hat. He stared at Hak Su with cold eyes and continued:
“Answer him, Senior Brother.”
A shock swept across the wall.
No, it was more than shock.
A man they believed dead had appeared before them.
While most stood frozen, Hak Su studied his Junior Brother in silence. Then he spoke calmly.
“I thought you were dead.”
“If that’s how it looked, then I was.”
Hak Eui’s face was set as he rubbed the neck that had supposedly been severed the night before.
“The fool who truly cared about you is already dead. And before dawn, I was born anew.”
“Then the head I saw...”
“You seem to have forgotten how crowded Xining’s underground prison is.”

Only then did Hak Su remember. A few days earlier, the Qinghai City Lord and several other leaders had been dragged into the streets and executed on the spot. Even after that, well over a hundred prisoners remained in the underground prison awaiting judgment.
And there was someone who could find one built like Hak Eui and make a human-skin mask convincing enough to fool them all.
“The Slaughter Saint.”
Hak Su murmured the name to himself and gave a small nod.
“So that’s what happened.”
His calm acceptance drew uneasy murmurs from those who had been watching, still hoping they were wrong.
Hak Su. It was him.
He was the traitor working with Dark Heaven.
The Kunlun Sect Leader’s Senior Disciple had betrayed the sect to which he had belonged for thirty years.
Cheongheoja looked at the Disciple he had wanted to believe in until the very end. His expression was impossible to describe.
Hak Su slowly opened his mouth.
“Do not ask why. Do not question. Think only of the mission you’ve been given.”
It was an answer, and a memory: words a child born in a land beyond the distant desert had heard countless times before he turned thirteen.
A duty and a mission etched into his bones, impossible to defy even after decades.
“Heaven above and earth below, let ten thousand demons bow in homage.”
“That is everything. I need no other reason.”
Hak Su looked directly into the trembling eyes of the man he had called Master. His face and voice were nothing like they had been before.
“I used to tell you that meeting you by Qinghai Lake was the greatest luck of my life.”
He had meant it.
No one deserved to be called a Daoist more than Cheongheoja. He had accepted his meeting with a boy wandering near Qinghai Lake as fate, never knowing the boy had made it look like chance.
“Thank you. I had no great martial talent. Even I never thought I’d rise this far.”
But Cheongheoja had cared nothing for status or talent. Even if the Kunlun Sect had not suffered such devastating losses in the Great Faction War, he would gladly have taken Hak Su as his Disciple.
Just as Hak Su had been raised to be a spy, Cheongheoja had always been that kind of man.
“It was all thanks to you, Cheongheoja.”
The instant a clear smile came to Hak Su’s lips—
“Hak Su, how dare you—!”
Hak Eui could bear no more. With an angry roar, he shot forward.
He was not the only one charging at the man who had betrayed their sect.
*Whoosh!*
Swift movement techniques. Formidable auras.
The Kunlun Ten Guests—regarded as the future Elders who would succeed the Kunlun Five Immortals, and as indispensable pillars of the sect—drew their swords without hesitation.
*Slice!*
A flash of steel cut into a torso. Hot blood gushed out.
*Splatter. Thud, thud.*
Blood sprayed across the wall.

“What...?”
“I was getting tired of being called Hak Su.”
Hak Su—or rather, Dark Heaven’s spy—looked at the five corpses lying with severed throats and pierced hearts. Then he slowly raised his head.
Beside him stood the other shadows who had infiltrated the Kunlun Sect before him, or around the same time.
“Number Six. That is my name.”
At that moment—

The Kunlun Five Guests—the five remaining members, spies raised by Dark Heaven—took the Temporary Strength Pills hidden in their robes and chewed them.
Sssssss!

“I truly cannot leave you behind.”

sentences.text: Xining Fortress, the last line of defense in Qinghai, was well suited to withstanding a siege.
But in the dozens of battles fought over the years, its high, sturdy walls had not been the only thing to give invaders nightmares.
“As expected, even those Fiends are having trouble crossing the moat.”
At the middle-aged Daoist’s admiring murmur, Cheongheoja, Sect Leader of the Kunlun Sect, nodded.
“Without it, this fight would be twice as hard.
The gate would have fallen long ago.”
Even now, the moat—which was more than ten jang wide and quite deep—was forcing the enemy to pay a terrible price.
And crossing it was only the beginning.
Beyond it waited a gate made of immensely thick black iron.
No matter how skilled Dark Heaven’s fanatics were in martial arts, they had little choice but to suffer the losses and scale the walls instead.
The walls had been in danger at times, thanks perhaps to the enemy’s overwhelming numbers and the strength granted by their Temporary Strength Pills.
But here at the East Gate, the defense was holding more easily than anywhere else.
If they could keep it that way, they might even win.
The middle-aged Daoist beside Cheongheoja seemed to share that hope.
“If we win this battle, we can all return to the main sect together, can’t we?”
“All of us together...
How wonderful that would be.”
Cheongheoja’s voice was heavier than ever.
The middle-aged Daoist’s expression turned bitter.
“Are you thinking about your second Disciple?”
Cheongheoja was silent for a moment, then shook his head.
“No.”
“Then...”
“I was thinking about the shortcomings of a foolish master who failed to guide his Disciple down the right path.”
“It was my fault.
From beginning to end.
All of it.”
“Master...”
The middle-aged Daoist—Cheongheoja’s Senior Disciple, Hak Su—looked at him with sorrow.
“Don’t blame yourself.
It wasn’t your fault.”
“Is that what you think?”
“I know it.
Everyone in Kunlun does.
You kept your second Disciple closer than anyone else and took special care of him.”
“I had to.
You were always gentle, and your third Junior Brother was full of energy.
But that child always seemed rough and unsettled.”
“Wasn’t that why you gave him the Daoist name Hak Eui?”
“Yes.
That was why.”
The boy who had grown up in dark, dangerous back alleys had gained a new name and a family.
Cheongheoja had always urged his rough-tempered second Disciple to live up to that name and become a more righteous man.
To never forget, even for an instant, that he was a Daoist.
“But... who could have guessed he was a spy conspiring with Dark Heaven?”
Hak Su pressed his lips together and shook his head.
“I still can’t believe it.
I don’t want to.”
His gaze shifted to the empty space beside him, as though his second Junior Brother might be standing there with his usual crooked look.
But that would never happen.
No.
It was impossible.
Hak Eui was already dead.
Before dawn, he had resisted those who came under cover of night to capture the spy.
In the end, he had lost his life.
Hak Su had arrived at the scene too late.
He’d seen his master holding his Junior Brother’s severed head and a sword dripping with blood.
He’d seen his master with eyes sadder than ever—just like now.
“Master...”
Just as Hak Su looked at Cheongheoja, torn by conflicting thoughts—
*Whoosh!*
A sharp whistle cut through the air.
A messenger came racing toward them, using his movement technique with all his might.
“Sect Leader!”
He was covered in blood, and his face was as white as a sheet.
Cheongheoja swallowed the groan that almost escaped him and spoke in a heavy voice.
“Where have you come from?”
“The South Gate.
Hah...
The South Gate.”
“Then the two Seniors have ordered a retreat to the Inner City?”
“How did you...?”
“I understand.
It must be much the same elsewhere.”
No further words were needed.
The messenger’s appearance had told Cheongheoja enough.
He went on calmly.
“Go and tell them I’ll lead the East Gate forces to the Inner City shortly.”
“May fortune favor you in battle.”
The messenger bowed briefly and left.
Hak Su’s face hardened.
“Go ahead without me.
I’ll stay with some of the troops and buy you time.”
His eyes and voice were full of resolve, but Cheongheoja shook his head at once.
“I can’t leave you behind.”
Hearing the concern in his master’s voice, Hak Su gave a faint smile.
“The road to the Inner City won’t be easy.
It may be even more dangerous than staying here.
They need you more than they need me.”
It was a reasonable prediction.
The dire news that the West Gate had fallen to the Blood Lord had reached the East Gate just before the war drums were about to be destroyed.

Unlike the East Gate, where the enemy forces were comparatively weaker than at the other three gates, a retreat without a plan might lead them straight into the Blood Lord and his fanatics, who could be rampaging unchecked through the fortress from the West Gate.
Even so, Cheongheoja would not yield.
“I forbid it.”
“Master, we’re out of time!”
Hak Su could no longer contain his urgency.
But then—
“Who is out of time?”
Cheongheoja’s voice sank strangely low, piercing Hak Su’s ear.
“Master...?”
“I asked who was out of time.”
Hak Su blinked at him, bewildered.
The old Daoist’s presence had changed so suddenly that the Kunlun Disciples who knew him well—and all the soldiers nearby—were staring at Cheongheoja.
Then an unexpected voice rang through the rain.
“Why hesitate?
Your master, lofty as the heavens, has asked you a question.”
*Splash.*
A foot came down in a puddle, accompanied by a hard-edged voice.
At the same time, a man who looked to be around thirty took off his low-pulled straw hat.
He stared at Hak Su with cold eyes and continued:
“Answer him, Senior Brother.”
A shock swept across the wall.
No, it was more than shock.
A man they believed dead had appeared before them.
While most stood frozen, Hak Su studied his Junior Brother in silence.
Then he spoke calmly.
“I thought you were dead.”
“If that’s how it looked, then I was.”
Hak Eui’s face was set as he rubbed the neck that had supposedly been severed the night before.
“The fool who truly cared about you is already dead.
And before dawn, I was born anew.”
“Then the head I saw...”
“You seem to have forgotten how crowded Xining’s underground prison is.”
Only then did Hak Su remember.
A few days earlier, the Qinghai City Lord and several other leaders had been dragged into the streets and executed on the spot.
Even after that, well over a hundred prisoners remained in the underground prison awaiting judgment.
And there was someone who could find one built like Hak Eui and make a human-skin mask convincing enough to fool them all.
“The Slaughter Saint.”
Hak Su murmured the name to himself and gave a small nod.
“So that’s what happened.”
His calm acceptance drew uneasy murmurs from those who had been watching, still hoping they were wrong.
Hak Su.
It was him.
He was the traitor working with Dark Heaven.
The Kunlun Sect Leader’s Senior Disciple had betrayed the sect to which he had belonged for thirty years.
Cheongheoja looked at the Disciple he had wanted to believe in until the very end.
His expression was impossible to describe.
Hak Su slowly opened his mouth.
“Do not ask why.

It was an answer, and a memory: words a child born in a land beyond the distant desert had heard countless times before he turned thirteen.
A duty and a mission etched into his bones, impossible to defy even after decades.
“Heaven above and earth below, let ten thousand demons bow in homage.”
“That is everything.
I need no other reason.”
Hak Su looked directly into the trembling eyes of the man he had called Master.

He had meant it.

Even I never thought I’d rise this far.”

Just as Hak Su had been raised to be a spy, Cheongheoja had always been that kind of man.

chapters.title: Chapter 1117
paragraphs: Today, there was nowhere in Xining where the word peace could be found.
Not to the east, west, south, or north. Not even in the sky.
Rain and blood drenched everything, while screams and crashes rang out without pause.
And yet there was one exception: a hill rising tall several hundred jang from the East Gate.
*It’s really coming down out there.*
Hardly the sort of thought someone in a life-or-death crisis could afford to have.
As he watched the sky pour down thick sheets of rain, as though a giant hole had opened overhead, the black-robed man suddenly turned east.
Whoooosh.
In the deep darkness, a fierce, stormlike wind whipped waves across the water.
After days of unprecedented rain without a moment’s pause, what had once been a fairly level stretch of ground had become something that could easily be called a river.
Of course, that wasn’t what the black-robed man was looking for.
“Have they arrived?”
His companion’s question came out of nowhere.
“Not yet.”
“They’re later than expected. They should’ve been here by now.”
“If they were diligent enough to keep to a schedule, why would they spend their lives robbing people?”
His companion gave a quiet laugh of agreement beneath his low-pulled black hood.
“But I didn’t think they’d be this stupid. They may be rootless bandits, but if they dare call themselves an Alliance, I thought they’d have at least a little skill or sense.”
“Maybe this is the result of them thinking things through, in their own way.”
“What do you mean?”
“Even fools can guess when they’re being used as cannon fodder. Most of them are petty bandits, but their leaders—the Seafaring King and the Green Forest Battle King—know how to use their heads.”
“So they’re deliberately dragging their feet to minimize their losses?”
“The weather’s gotten worse, too, but it’s certainly possible.”
“Even with nearly ten thousand of our people watching those bandits?”
“Who knows? Those water ghosts of the Yangtze River Channel League might pull something if they put their minds to it, no matter how closely we watch.”
“Ha. If that’s true, they’re not just stupid. They’re beyond saving.”
The black-robed man nodded as his companion clicked his tongue.
Neither had said it outright, but everyone in Dark Heaven knew how cruel the Blood Lord could be once he began rampaging with no thought for what came after.
If the combined forces of the Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance arrived only after the fighting was over...
*After today, the Central Plains will be clean. You won’t find so much as a hair from one of those bandits.*
But they still had a chance to survive.
If they arrived in time, before the East Gate opened as planned, and earned even a little credit to save face, they might extend their stubborn lives a while longer.
Of course, that depended on the Blood Lord’s mood.
*If you want to live, row with every last bit of strength you’ve got. It’ll save us both a headache.*
The black-robed man looked toward the East Gate, where the battle was raging.
What did he care whether a bunch of bandits lived or died? But for someone Dark Heaven classified as a corpse sorcerer, it mattered quite a lot.
His role was less that of a soldier fighting on the battlefield than a member of the crew hauling away the corpses scattered across it.
And while he worried about the extra work, the battle around the East Gate, which had been seesawing back and forth, suddenly took a sharp turn.
BOOOOM!
A deafening crash rang out.
It swallowed the sound of the rain and even the occasional thunder. The black-robed man and his companion stared wide-eyed.
The top of the fortress wall was collapsing amid a burst of light.
“What was that...?”
The black-robed man’s words came out as a groan.
The flash had lasted only an instant, but he was sure. The destructive energy still flaring across the wall was Force.
*Why? We haven’t even pressed the attack. Why would Cheongheoja...?*
The Kunlun Sect Leader came to mind, but the black-robed man shook his head.
POP! RUMMMBLE!
Another distant flash burst into view. Its pale, ominous light could hardly have come from Daoist martial arts.
“It’s not the Black Ghosts, either. They’re still holding their positions as ordered.”
His companion was right.
The two Black Ghosts were waiting on the battlefield in front of the wall, along with a considerable number of troops the Blood Lord had deliberately held back.
“Which means...”
The black-robed man stopped.
If that Force belonged to neither Cheongheoja nor a Black Ghost, there was only one possibility.
Spies.
The spies they had planted in the Kunlun Sect over many years had finally made their move—a step ahead of schedule.
“What do we do?”
The black-robed man bit his lip.
It was a real pain in the ass.

The combined forces of the Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance, who should have arrived at the battlefield by now, were still nowhere to be seen. Meanwhile, the spies who were supposed to open the East Gate were caught up in an unexpected fight.
To make matters worse, Ma Sanbao—effectively their direct superior—wasn’t there today. The black-robed man would have to make the call himself.
And fast.
He stared at the East Gate, torn between his options. The moment was brief, though it felt like an eternity. Then his eyes widened.
CLANK. GRRRRNNG!
The iron bridge began to move with a heavy grinding sound.
The massive bridge connected to the moat in front of the gate. It was coming down like a ray of light.
*The bridge is connected to the gate. It can only be operated from inside.*
It was clear proof that the spies planted in the Kunlun Sect were opening the gate—and the perfect opportunity.
There was no point hesitating any longer.
“I command you: answer the call!”
The black-robed man pulled the ritual bell from his belt and shook it hard.
Wooooong.
A sinister sound carried on the wind, its vibrations spreading outward.
The hill they had been standing on answered. Or rather, the enormous masses of flesh that the rain and chaos had made look like a hill did.
GRRRRKK!
The ground shook as if an earthquake had struck. A horrible corpse stench rose through the rain and mud.
BOOM. BOOOOM!
The monsters shook off the mud plastered over their bodies and stood on limbs as thick as great trees. There were a thousand in all.
Perched on one monster’s shoulder, the black-robed man shook his ritual bell again and whispered, “Wipe them all out.”
At that instant—
—KROOOAAAR!
With a roar as immense as their bodies, a thousand monsters surged toward the battlefield like a wave.
THUDDUDDUDDUD!
Was this what the Yellow River would look like in flood?
Screams rose belatedly from the wall as the defenders spotted the monsters bearing down on them with unstoppable momentum. But those weren’t the only enemies they had to face.
“All. Troops.”
“Charge.”
A low voice emerged from beneath black armor.
At the same time, the two Black Ghosts who had been waiting sprang forward.
SHWOOOSH!
A ghost horse, its white bones exposed, raced ahead like the wind. Several thousand fanatics charged behind it, their cries shaking the battlefield.
“Heaven above and earth below! Let ten thousand demons bow in homage!”
“The Lord of Heaven is with us!”
The immense shouts behind him sent a thrilling shiver up the black-robed man’s spine.
Things had strayed a little from the original plan, but those minor setbacks no longer mattered.
He had an army at his back. And beyond the iron bridge, which had descended nearly halfway...
*I see it!*
There was no doubt. He wasn’t seeing things.
As the iron bridge lowered on its chains, the enormous iron gate began to open. The sight was clear in the black-robed man’s eyes, brimming with delight.
Tss-tss-tss-tss!
The two corpse sorcerers shook their ritual bells with confident sweeps of their hands. The monsters pushed themselves to their limit and shot toward the East Gate.
*We can do this.*
Time seemed to slow. The black-robed man held his breath and watched the battlefield.
Flashes of light flickered without pause atop the wall, which was shrouded in crashes and dust. The bridge, more than halfway down, now covered the moat.
Only a little over a hundred jang remained.
*Faster. Faster...!*
The monsters leading the charge thundered forward, their footsteps like thunderclaps. Beside them, the ghost horse carrying the two Black Ghosts galloped as if it were a specter.
Whoooosh!
A fierce wind wrapped around the black-robed man. His heart pounded as the distance shrank.
A little over a hundred jang became half that.
Then half again.
And at last—
GRRRNNG. BOOM!
The long, sturdy iron bridge settled over the moat.
BOOOOM!
The two Black Ghosts crossed first. Behind them, a thousand monsters surged toward the wide-open gate like one enormous spear.
KRRRRRUNCH!
A terrifying crash sent dust billowing into the air. The black-robed man and his companion had finally broken through the barrier of the East Gate, and they let out the breaths they had been holding.
They had done it. By their own strength.
No one could dispute their success—or the magnitude of their feat.
Even the merciless Blood Lord would have to acknowledge it.
For that moment, at least, both men could rejoice.
SHWING—BOOM!
Then a dazzling flash of Force flew in from somewhere and shattered the thick chain connecting the gate and the iron bridge.
CLANK. RRRRRK!
It happened too quickly for anyone to react.
The two corpse sorcerers stared blankly as the heavy gate began to close. Beyond the settling dust, a hazy figure came into view.
SPLASH. SPLASH.
Staggering steps. A robe soaked in blood.
Then the middle-aged man’s face emerged, his eyes glowing red as if to prove he had committed a forbidden act.
The black-robed man slowly parted his lips.
At that moment—
Slice!
A streak of light cut through the dust and across the middle-aged man’s—no, Hak Su’s—neck.
A voice rang out, thick with sorrow and anger.
“By the solemn rules of the Great Kunlun Sect, I execute the criminals of our sect.”
THUD. FWOOSH.
The headless body collapsed, and the dust cloud parted.
Only then did the two corpse sorcerers see their surroundings clearly. Only then did they understand.
The spies hadn’t lowered the bridge and opened the gate. The defenders of the East Gate had.
*A trap...!*
The realization struck like lightning.
But the shock lasted only a moment. There were fewer than three thousand defenders, and Cheongheoja looked exhausted. The black-robed man’s lips twisted into a grin.
“You dare try such a shoddy trick?”
It was a trap—but at the same time, it wasn’t.
The gate had shut out the fanatics following them, but their strongest forces—the Black Ghosts and the monsters—were already inside.
“Did you think this would stop us?”
A young man standing beside Cheongheoja answered his scornful question.
“Why not? We’ve been through a whole lot worse. Right, everyone?”
The black-robed man frowned at him. There was something about the young man’s face that made him want to torment him.
Just then, a young beggar with grime streaming down his face spoke up.
“Quit calling me a beggar. It hurts the feelings of the beggar listening.”
“Who the hell are you...?”
“Honestly, we end up in situations like this every time. I can’t even figure out how much extra pay we’re owed anymore.”
A cold-faced young man cut him off. Then a clear voice, utterly at odds with the mood, rang out.
“But we always made it through. Together.”
“True, but this time is different. The most important person isn’t here.”
“Right. Taishan wants to eat Pavilion Master. Old Man Nam, too.”
“Taishan. You mean you miss them, not that you want to eat them.”
“Oh. Got mixed up. My lord is smart, as expected.”
“Not bad. Still, not as good as me.”
Young men and women the corpse sorcerers had never seen before. A hulking man who looked none too bright. A wild-haired eccentric.
Faced with the bizarre sight, the two sorcerers couldn’t think of anything to ask.
More precisely, they didn’t think it was worth asking.
“Wipe them all out.”
The ritual bell began to move with his quiet mutter.
Boooooo!
A horn sounded in the distance, and everyone at the East Gate stopped moving.
For some, that sound meant hope. For others, utter despair.
“The Yangtze River Channel League...”
Someone’s low groan hung heavily in the air.

Was this what the Yellow River would look like in flood?
Screams rose belatedly from the wall as the defenders spotted the monsters bearing down on them with unstoppable momentum.
But those weren’t the only enemies they had to face.
“All.
Troops.”
“Charge.”
A low voice emerged from beneath black armor.
At the same time, the two Black Ghosts who had been waiting sprang forward.
SHWOOOSH!
A ghost horse, its white bones exposed, raced ahead like the wind.
Several thousand fanatics charged behind it, their cries shaking the battlefield.
“Heaven above and earth below!
Let ten thousand demons bow in homage!”
“The Lord of Heaven is with us!”
The immense shouts behind him sent a thrilling shiver up the black-robed man’s spine.
Things had strayed a little from the original plan, but those minor setbacks no longer mattered.
He had an army at his back.
And beyond the iron bridge, which had descended nearly halfway...
*I see it!*
There was no doubt.
He wasn’t seeing things.
As the iron bridge lowered on its chains, the enormous iron gate began to open.
The sight was clear in the black-robed man’s eyes, brimming with delight.
Tss-tss-tss-tss!
The two corpse sorcerers shook their ritual bells with confident sweeps of their hands.
The monsters pushed themselves to their limit and shot toward the East Gate.
*We can do this.*
Time seemed to slow.
The black-robed man held his breath and watched the battlefield.
Flashes of light flickered without pause atop the wall, which was shrouded in crashes and dust.
The bridge, more than halfway down, now covered the moat.
Only a little over a hundred jang remained.
*Faster.
Faster...!*
The monsters leading the charge thundered forward, their footsteps like thunderclaps.
Beside them, the ghost horse carrying the two Black Ghosts galloped as if it were a specter.
Whoooosh!
A fierce wind wrapped around the black-robed man.
His heart pounded as the distance shrank.
A little over a hundred jang became half that.
Then half again.
And at last—
GRRRNNG.
BOOM!
The long, sturdy iron bridge settled over the moat.
BOOOOM!
The two Black Ghosts crossed first.
Behind them, a thousand monsters surged toward the wide-open gate like one enormous spear.
KRRRRRUNCH!
A terrifying crash sent dust billowing into the air.
The black-robed man and his companion had finally broken through the barrier of the East Gate, and they let out the breaths they had been holding.
They had done it.
By their own strength.
No one could dispute their success—or the magnitude of their feat.
Even the merciless Blood Lord would have to acknowledge it.
For that moment, at least, both men could rejoice.
SHWING—BOOM!
Then a dazzling flash of Force flew in from somewhere and shattered the thick chain connecting the gate and the iron bridge.
CLANK.
RRRRRK!
It happened too quickly for anyone to react.
The two corpse sorcerers stared blankly as the heavy gate began to close.
Beyond the settling dust, a hazy figure came into view.
SPLASH.
SPLASH.
Staggering steps.
A robe soaked in blood.
Then the middle-aged man’s face emerged, his eyes glowing red as if to prove he had committed a forbidden act.
The black-robed man slowly parted his lips.
At that moment—
Slice!
A streak of light cut through the dust and across the middle-aged man’s—no, Hak Su’s—neck.
A voice rang out, thick with sorrow and anger.
“By the solemn rules of the Great Kunlun Sect, I execute the criminals of our sect.”
THUD.
FWOOSH.
The headless body collapsed, and the dust cloud parted.
Only then did the two corpse sorcerers see their surroundings clearly.
Only then did they understand.
The spies hadn’t lowered the bridge and opened the gate.
The defenders of the East Gate had.
*A trap...!*
The realization struck like lightning.
But the shock lasted only a moment.
There were fewer than three thousand defenders, and Cheongheoja looked exhausted.
The black-robed man’s lips twisted into a grin.
“You dare try such a shoddy trick?”
It was a trap—but at the same time, it wasn’t.
The gate had shut out the fanatics following them, but their strongest forces—the Black Ghosts and the monsters—were already inside.
“Did you think this would stop us?”
A young man standing beside Cheongheoja answered his scornful question.
“Why not?
We’ve been through a whole lot worse.
Right, everyone?”
The black-robed man frowned at him.
There was something about the young man’s face that made him want to torment him.
Just then, a young beggar with grime streaming down his face spoke up.
“Quit calling me a beggar.
It hurts the feelings of the beggar listening.”
“Who the hell are you...?”
“Honestly, we end up in situations like this every time.
I can’t even figure out how much extra pay we’re owed anymore.”
A cold-faced young man cut him off.
Then a clear voice, utterly at odds with the mood, rang out.
“But we always made it through.
Together.”
“True, but this time is different.
The most important person isn’t here.”
“Right.
Taishan wants to eat Pavilion Master.
Old Man Nam, too.”
“Taishan.
You mean you miss them, not that you want to eat them.”
“Oh.
Got mixed up.
My lord is smart, as expected.”
“Not bad.
Still, not as good as me.”
Young men and women the corpse sorcerers had never seen before.
A hulking man who looked none too bright.
A wild-haired eccentric.
Faced with the bizarre sight, the two sorcerers couldn’t think of anything to ask.
More precisely, they didn’t think it was worth asking.
“Wipe them all out.”
The ritual bell began to move with his quiet mutter.
Boooooo!
A horn sounded in the distance, and everyone at the East Gate stopped moving.
For some, that sound meant hope.
For others, utter despair.
“The Yangtze River Channel League...”
Someone’s low groan hung heavily in the air.

chapters.title: Chapter 1118
paragraphs: Boooooo!
The horn sounded far away, reaching the defenders at the East Gate. For a moment, they found themselves wishing it belonged to reinforcements coming to help them.
But the truth was cruel and unmistakable.
“The Yangtze River Channel League...”
The groan that slipped from someone’s lips spoke for every defender there.
They could not see its source, but they heard it clearly.
Not the west. Not the south. Not the north.
It came from beyond the East Gate wall where they stood. That could mean only one thing.
*They’re here.*
Everyone knew who was coming from the east.
The Green Forest Alliance and the Yangtze River Channel League.
Two vast bands of outlaws who roamed the broad, blue rivers and mountains, yet still wanted a piece of the world itself.
And with them would come the forces of Dark Heaven.
An enemy army estimated at thirty thousand had finally arrived, following the long course of the Yangtze and pushing upstream against the Yellow River’s mighty current.
As the defenders fell silent before that reality, the two corpse sorcerers twisted their mouths into grins.
“You fools.”
“Do you understand now how shallow your little scheme was?”
The black-robed man and his companion made no effort to hide their delight.

They might have fallen for the defenders’ trap and ended up inside the fortress, but their forces were strong enough to overcome a three-to-one disadvantage. Now tens of thousands of reinforcements had arrived at just the right time. They were almost embarrassed to remember how tense they’d been when they realized they were trapped.
*The Lord of Heaven truly is helping us.*
The black-robed man smiled faintly at the thought of the new heaven he served. Then—
*Step.*
A group moved forward. They ought to have retreated at once, but instead, they came closer.
*Of course. I knew the Kunlun fools would come out like this.*
He spotted Cheongheoja and the Kunlun Disciples at the front and nodded to himself. Then several others popped out beside them, and he sighed.
“I’ve been meaning to ask... Who the hell are you people?”
If they’d looked ordinary, he wouldn’t have given them a second thought. But even to a corpse sorcerer, the seven men and women made up a bizarre group.
Unfazed, they answered—or rather, the young man at their center spoke for them.
“Swift Wind Sword Hyuk Mujin. That’s who I am.”
The black-robed man’s eyes widened.
“Swift Wind Sword?”
“That’s right. So you’ve heard of—”
“Never heard of you.”
“...Fine. Let me introduce myself again. I’m Hyuk Mujin, Vice Squad Leader of the Jin Dragon Squad. Though I’m taking a break from that for now.”
“I haven’t heard of that either. You might as well keep taking a break. Not that you’ll be in this world after today.”
“...Damn it. Then how about Hyuk Mujin, Vice Captain of the Fire Dragon Pavilion?”
This time, his companions’ eyes widened.
“What? Since when? Do Vice Captains get extra pay?”
“Why would they choose Warrior Hyuk, of all people? Wasn’t the position vacant?”
“I don’t know. Honestly, I thought I was the best fit among us, but it seems I’ve been passed over because I’m from the unorthodox faction.”
“Discrimination. Know. Delicious.”
“Is this guy possessed by a glutton? In all my life, I’ve never met anyone more of a beggar than my Master.”
“Oh, so your Master’s a beggar too. No wonder. The moment I saw you, I thought you looked like you’d be good at begging for a living.”

Greed and distrust they couldn’t hide even now. Disappointment with the orthodox faction’s rigged playing field. Endless appetite. And last of all, disrespect toward their Master and a steady stream of rudeness, as natural as breathing.
The black-robed man and his companion felt dizzy, as though they were staring into a true abyss. If not for Hyuk Mujin’s answer, they might not have dared open their mouths.
But *Fire Dragon Pavilion* was familiar even to them. Everyone in Dark Heaven knew the name, regardless of rank, because of its connection to one particular man.
“The Fire Dragon Pavilion... You’re Jin Taekyung’s people?”
Hyuk Mujin gave his companions a cool look, then answered solemnly.
“That’s right.”
“Thanks, but strictly speaking, I’m with the Beggars’ Sect, not the Fire Dragon Pavilion.”
“Neither am I. I think.”
“...Could the two of you please keep your mouths shut? Please?”
The black-robed man looked them over again.

His duties hadn’t required him to know minor details like Swift Wind Sword or the Jin Dragon Squad, but he knew of the Fire Dragon Pavilion. Whenever Jin Taekyung had stood in the way of Dark Heaven’s grand plans, the Fire Dragon Pavilion had helped him, and its reputation had spread throughout the world.

He didn’t know why the one who looked most like a nobody was its Vice Captain. Still, he could see how this strange assortment had ended up together—and why they dared step forward in a situation like this.
“Birds of a feather flock together. You’ve gathered all the crazy men and women who don’t value their lives, just like your Pavilion Master.”
The black-robed man let out a short laugh.
The Fire Dragon Pavilion? He’d admit they had been a thorn in Dark Heaven’s side. But only because Jin Taekyung had been there.

Without him, the people before the black-robed man were merely young prodigies who had yet to come into their own. Puppies drunk on bravado and dreams of heroism, unable to tell when to advance and when to retreat.
“You spent your chance to run spouting nonsense. That’s why you’re going to die.”
What more was there to say to puppies whose teeth hadn’t even come in? An old, wounded beast quietly gathering its strength for one final struggle would be another matter.
*There’s a Supreme Peak master among them. We still can’t let our guard down.*
*You worry too much. With the forces they have, they can’t get through the monsters to hurt us.*
The black-robed man and his companion exchanged a silent glance. Watching Cheongheoja and the Kunlun Disciples aim their swords at them, they raised the ritual bells in their hands.
Tss-tss-tss-tss.
—Grrrrrr.
The thousand monsters growled in response to the waves from the bells.

Each was as large as two grown men put together. Their bodies were so tough, and healed so quickly, that nothing short of the level of injuring others with Sword Energy could leave a fatal wound. Ready to lunge, they fixed their eyes on the defenders.
Ssshhhh.

Beside them, the two Black Ghosts radiated a terrifying energy. Together, they gave off such overwhelming killing intent that even the defenders, resolved to fight to the death, instinctively stepped back.
Then, at last—
“Kill every last one of them.”
At the cold command, the two corpse sorcerers swept their ritual bells through the air.
Tss-tss-tss-tss-tss.
The cursed sound waves, branded deep in the souls of the Black Ghosts and monsters, swept across the East Gate.
From beyond it came a quiet voice.
“Why would we run? We need to buy time by spouting whatever bullshit we can.”
The black-robed man and his companion stopped without realizing it and blinked.
Was it because they couldn’t understand the words of that nobody—Hyuk Mujin, who’d butted in out of habit and now claimed to be the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s Vice Captain?
No.
The Black Ghosts were charging toward the defenders. The thousand monsters were not. Their limbs trembled as though something invisible held them in place.
*I gave the command... So why?*
Just as the question struck the two corpse sorcerers—
“Hey, can’t you do it?”
Hyuk Mujin turned, and someone appeared behind him. Someone the two sorcerers had never expected to see here.
“I tried to focus as hard as I could. Hngh. But there’s no way I can manage the Black Ghosts...”
His voice trailed off as their eyes met.

The two corpse sorcerers stared wide-eyed at their missing companion. They’d thought he would be dead by now. Ever since the Slaughter Saint had captured him at Qinghai Lake, he’d vanished without a trace.
Then they saw the dozen or so ritual bells in his hands. The bells had clearly belonged to the other corpse sorcerers who had died near Qinghai Lake. A sad smile spread across his bruised face.
“Sorry. That’s how it went.”
At that moment—
SHWEEEE!
A dazzling streak of light cut through the darkness and blocked the two Black Ghosts, who were racing forward like the wind alongside their ghost horse.
KWA-BOOM!
A deafening crash sent wind sweeping in every direction.
At the same time, through the thick cloud of dust, Cheongheoja and a wild-haired eccentric—no, a Great Sir—appeared and spoke to the Black Ghosts.
“Where do you think you’re going?”
“Couldn’t we talk this over first...? Oh, that was quite a good line.”
The two corpse sorcerers gritted their teeth. Amid the frantic fighting at the four walls, they had failed to notice another Supreme Peak master.
Perhaps what angered them most, though, was the insolent smile on that nobody’s face.
“If Captain—no, if the Pavilion Master were here, he’d say this.”
At Hyuk Mujin’s gesture, the captured corpse sorcerer shook the bells in both hands like mad.
Not one bell. More than ten.
Tss-tss-tss-tss!
The desperate jingle, driven by a stronger instinct to survive than at any other point in his life, pushed him one step beyond the limit of his usual ability.
In other words—
—Ghk, grrk?
He could not wrest complete control from the two corpse sorcerers who had been his companions yesterday and were his enemies today. But he could throw the thousand monsters into confusion.
—Kraaaagh!
—Gueeeeee!
Red eyes flashed wildly. Their killing intent lost its original target.
THOOM!
KRRRUNCH!

Freed from whatever had held them still, the monsters rampaged without distinguishing friend from foe. As the two corpse sorcerers froze at the sight, Hyuk Mujin’s words struck their ears like arrows.
“From now on, kill each other.”
Boooooo!
Over the horn sounding ever closer by the moment, the monsters’ ferocious roars mingled with the defenders’ shouts.

chapters.title: Chapter 1119
paragraphs: BOOOOM!
A deafening crash rang out, and the ground shook.

A thousand monsters rampaged without distinguishing friend from foe. Three thousand defenders stood ready to fight to the death. And four Supreme Peak masters flashed across the battlefield, clashing again and again.
The battle around the East Gate began in greater chaos and brutality than ever before.
Even the man who had designed and set this whole situation in motion could barely suppress his fear, despite putting all his strength into it.
—Kyaaaaa!
Hyuk Mujin watched the monsters charge, his eyes trembling as they roared.
They stood over one jang tall, with limbs as thick as the trunks of great trees. Their strength and speed far exceeded human limits. Their charge felt like a wave nothing could stop.
*How has Captain fought so many of these things?*
Jin Taekyung came to mind at once. He had always fought at the front, at the center of everyone else, risking his life.
And Mujin understood all over again why he had survived so many crises. He understood the enormous gap Taekyung had filled alone, and the weight of the responsibility he had carried.
*So this is what it felt like.*
Hyuk Mujin let out a ragged breath. His question would never reach Taekyung.
He was afraid. Afraid enough to throw down his sword and run as far as he could.
*I would have done it before. No question.*
But things had changed. The heir to a venerable fabric shop had become a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, and he had come too far to turn and run.
The people who had gladly taken him along despite his lack of talent and skill had taught him too much. Jin Taekyung most of all.
“Never retreat.”
The words slipped past his trembling lips. They were less a command to the allies around him than a vow to himself.
They were also words the reckless Third Young Master—who now existed only in Mujin’s memories—had once said to him.
“Once you retreat... you’ll never be able to move forward again.”
So Hyuk Mujin did not retreat.
He suppressed the fear surging up from the depths of his chest, steadied his trembling sword tip, and charged at the monsters with all his might, roaring at the top of his lungs.
Just as Jin Taekyung had. Just as the other companions who had always believed in him did.
SHWEEEE!
A fierce wind whirled around him, wrapping his entire body.
Anyone who has experienced war agrees on one thing.

Battle was another word for madness, and war was all that madness gathered in one place. Keep cutting down the enemy before you and dodging the attacks that never stopped coming, and soon you would forget everything you knew.
Mujin clearly remembered hearing those words from an elderly man when he was a child.
He also remembered what the old man had told him when Mujin declared he would become a martial artist.
*Hope is dazzling, but reality is cruel.*
Yes. That was probably how he’d put it.
Now Mujin felt the truth of those words down to his bones.
THUD!
A heavy blow sent a shock through his entire body.
He had no time to react. Even if he had, he could not have dodged it completely. His strength had run out long ago.
KRRRUNCH!
How many times had the sky and ground turned over in his vision, bleached white? The first thing Hyuk Mujin felt after he was flung a long way was pain, great and small, sweeping through his body.
Blood came up with his cough and ran from the corner of his mouth.
His aching joints and twisted innards told him the truth: he was in terrible shape.
*Damn... it.*
Mujin gritted his teeth and swallowed the blood rising in his throat.
The old man’s face had long since faded from his memory, but his words had not. Reality was cruel.
To Mujin, at least.
*Only fifteen minutes, and look at me.*
He could barely make his body move. A weak, self-mocking laugh escaped him.
Losing control had not made the monsters any less powerful. The creatures Dark Heaven had made were as strong as they were hideous.
Without the fine sword still in his hand, Mujin doubted he could have brought down twenty of them on his own.
*Come to think of it, I only managed that much because of Captain.*
He looked at the blade. Even after cutting through the monsters’ tough bones and flesh, it had lost none of its keen edge.

The sword had been forged from part of the iron chain Jin Taekyung had given him after finally breaking free of his iron balls, just before the Star-Array Grand Banquet. It was the very chain the Fire Gate Clan had made to bind criminals of its own sect.
Only part of that chain had gone into the blade, but it contained a full four nyang of Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron. Its strength and sharpness made it worthy of being called a fine sword.

People who knew its origins sometimes teased Mujin that the sword was too good for him. He always bristled, but deep down, he knew they had a point. He had been stuck in the First Rate realm, making no progress. He owned a sword this precious only because Taekyung cared for his subordinate.
“Always snapping at people... and still making sure they have everything they need.”
Mujin gave a faint, amused snort and slowly forced his screaming body upright.
Then he wrung out what strength remained and rushed the nearest enemy from behind.
Slice!
Perhaps it was exhaustion. His sword tip wavered at the last moment, but it still cut through his target’s neck. This enemy, after all, was made of flesh and blood like Mujin.
SPLAT.
The headless fanatic staggered and fell into a pool of blood. Looking down at the body, Mujin felt his heart sink.
*If only we’d had a little more strength. Just a little...*

The strategy using the captured corpse sorcerer had worked. Most of the thousand monsters had fallen into confusion, and the three thousand defenders had charged into the chaos, driving their enemies back without regard for their own lives.
But the enemies they faced were not all inside the walls.

While the East Gate defenders gave everything they had to fighting the monsters, Dark Heaven’s fanatics climbed over the walls using hooks and ladders. The moment they entered the battle, they tipped the balance away from the defenders.
Even now—
The eight-character creed, steeped in madness and all too familiar by now, rang out with a muffled force.
Mujin saw fanatics pouring down from the walls. He saw his exhausted allies, and the monsters beginning, one by one, to come back to their senses.
He heard the strong blare of a horn, now only a few hundred jang away. And he saw the face of someone who had recovered his smile as though nothing had happened.
“Your struggle ends here.”
Mujin could not hear the words. But he could see the black-robed man’s lips moving far away, before the tightly shut gate.

The man’s companion had been killed by the monsters under his command as soon as the battle began. This sorcerer had managed to retain some control. Dozens of monsters still shielded him, and he was alive to enjoy a victory that, after one brief scare, seemed all but certain.
*Yeah, maybe it really is over. But...*
If Mujin ran away here, where would he ever win?
Hyuk Mujin muttered to himself as he staggered forward.
Forward, not back.
Whoooosh!
Even through his dulled senses, he felt the violent rush of air. A monster’s fist, backed by hundreds of geun of force, came down toward the crown of his head. It would crush him in an instant.
Then—
Slice.
A sharp streak of Sword Energy came from somewhere and split the thick bone and flesh.
“It’s too late. If you don’t want to die, get back! Now!”
That face. That voice.
But Hyuk Mujin did not stop for Song Ilseom’s warning. More precisely, he heard nothing at all.
At that moment, only one person’s voice echoed in his ears like a hallucination.
“Mujin.”
Jin Taekyung.
The man Mujin wanted to be like more than anyone—and the man who had shown him that he never could be.
Mujin moved his lips, stiff with dried blood, remembering their conversation before the battle.
“Yes. Go ahead.”
SHWICK!
The hiss of something cutting through the air from his blind spot answered him instead. But Song Ilseom was not the only one who wanted Mujin to live.
THUNK!
A fanatic charging Mujin from the side arched backward like a bow.
Ju Hwaran drew her sword from the collapsing man’s back. A dozen or so enemies who had been moving to stop Mujin changed direction and rushed her instead.
KRRRANG!
Steel rang out amid the unending screams and shouts. Mujin walked as though entranced along the path they had opened wider for him.
He left everything around him behind and listened to the voice still ringing in his ears.
“If something goes wrong—I mean, on the slightest chance that it does...”
Taekyung had been different then. There had been no laughter in his face, no trace of mischief.
“At least die where I can see you.”
And then, facing his subordinate, who had gone rigid, he’d forced a strained smile.
“Of course, that won’t happen. But if it did, I’d be able to avenge you, wouldn’t I?”
It was the first time Taekyung had said anything like that.
Through all the dangers they had survived together, he had only ever told Mujin one of two things.
Run.
Or make sure you survive.
Whatever danger came, Taekyung was always the one at the center, the one out in front. He had never hesitated to take the lead in this damn gamble they played with their lives.
To protect a subordinate, a companion, his master—or someone he had never even met.
Mujin could not help respecting him. And he could not help giving him the answer he wanted.
“Of course we’ll win this time, too. But yes. If it comes to that, I promise I will.”
Perhaps that was when Mujin had first begun quietly turning the word *death* over in his mind. When he had truly prepared himself to die.
But...
*If I’m going to die, I won’t die for nothing.*
He forced up a corner of his blood-crusted mouth and brought down the sword in his clenched hand.
Slice!
The two fanatics blocking his path fell at the same time, as though they had planned it. So easily that it looked like a scene from a play.
Then, at the fanatics who had stopped short, eyes wide at this unexpected turn, a fierce torrent of saber energy swept in.
KRRRUNCH!
Beneath a fountain of blood came a cold voice, strangely at odds with the ferocity of the attack.
“Go. If that’s your choice... I’ll open the way.”
That was all.
Sama Pyo plunged among the enemy without hesitation. A strong hand caught Mujin’s shoulder as he stumbled.
“Hyuk Mu...”
Mujin quietly shook his head at Taishan.
He knew what Taishan wanted to say. Killing the black-robed corpse sorcerer, now just twenty jang away, would not change who won this battle.
But Taekyung would have said that even if they died, the trade would be worth it.
“Hur...ry.”
It took nearly all Mujin’s strength to get the word out.
Taishan watched him silently, then tightened his grip. And with one short sentence, he used all his strength to send Mujin flying far away.
“Let’s go eat something good later, Vice Captain.”
SHWEEEE!
Wind tore past Mujin’s body. He answered Taishan in his heart.
*We will. We’ll eat until we burst.*
And then the black-robed man’s wide eyes were right in front of him.
Slice!
A flash carrying the last of Mujin’s strength swept across the corpse sorcerer’s neck.
In a battle where thousands—tens of thousands—were locked together, one person’s death might mean nothing.
But the single head rising into the air was enough to change the battle around the East Gate.
Thud. Clatter.
The head fell. The ritual bell dropped from the dead man’s loosened hand.
At the same instant, the roughly three hundred monsters that had survived the terrible melee and were still rampaging stopped moving.
For one stretched-thin instant, silence fell.
Some stared wide-eyed. Some smiled faintly.
And someone else, who had made all of this possible, felt a shiver run down his spine as he silently looked at the head at his feet.
No—not at the head. At the clean cut across the corpse sorcerer’s neck.
At the trace of what people under heaven called Sword Energy.
*It wasn’t the sword...*
It had happened for only an instant. Perhaps, with his mind already half gone, he had imagined it.
That did not matter. He had finally done it with his own strength.
He had proved, at least a little, why he’d been able to defeat twenty monsters, and why he deserved to stand alongside companions who were far more than he could ever hope to deserve.
And just as a feeble smile formed on Hyuk Mujin’s lips—
BOOOOM!
A blast like the sky splitting open shook heaven and earth. An immense wave of qi flung open the tightly shut gate.
Wooooooong.
The air trembled.
Through the faint darkness, a shadow wreathed in an aura as immense as a mountain leaned toward Hyuk Mujin, standing alone before the gate.
“What is your name?”
In that moment, Mujin knew this was where his life would end. He would not be able to keep the promise he had made to Taekyung before the battle.
“Fire Dragon Pavilion... No. Swift Wind Sword Hyuk Mujin.”
He answered more calmly than he ever had before.
Then, with the shadow’s quiet reply, he felt an immense force drive into his chest.
“I’ll remember it.”
POOM!
Hyuk Mujin’s vision plunged into darkness.

paragraphs: Boom!
The low sound of air being torn apart rang out, and the whole world seemed to stop.
At least, that was how it felt to the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion who saw a palm strike, launched at lightning speed, hit Hyuk Mujin in the chest.
And then—
Splatter.
As Hyuk Mujin’s body crumpled, scattering dark-red blood, the world that had stopped began to move again.
“No!”
Taishan’s eyes were bloodshot. The muscles across his body bulged as if they might burst.
At the unbelievable sight before him, he let out a thunderous roar and charged toward the gate.
He forgot his exhaustion. He cast aside his fear.
Like an enraged bull, Taishan swung his two-section staff with all his strength and pressed forward.
Whoooosh! Wham!
Each time the furious wind rose, brains flew and bones shattered like powder.
Fanatics had taken the place of the monsters, frozen like statues at the death of the corpse sorcerer. They tried to block his path, but none could easily stop Taishan in his rage.
No—more accurately, they couldn’t stop *them*.
KRRRUNCH!
A fierce rush of saber energy tore through the space, and severed limbs flew in every direction.
Amid the swirling spray of blood, Sama Pyo’s eyes—usually so composed—blazed with blue fire.
And someone else plunged into the dozens of fanatics closing in around Sama Pyo, heedless of their fallen comrades.
SHWEEEE!
Song Ilseom’s narrow-bladed sword shot through the air in swift, economical movements, each one utterly cruel.
Even the epithet Soul-Chasing Guest seemed inadequate.
Stab! Stab-stab!
Song Ilseom stabbed and twisted at every opening.
With the most efficient movements, he dealt his enemies certain pain and death.

Blood burst from a terrible scream and splashed across his face. Blades rained down indiscriminately from every direction, leaving cuts large and small across his body. But his tightly pressed lips didn’t tremble.
The blood flowing through Song Ilseom’s veins came from an illustrious family. But what had made him the Soul-Chasing Guest was blood shed on the battlefield.

He had once left the path of the wandering martial artist, which he’d walked all his life to repay the debt of an earlier generation. Now he was throwing his life away to repay a comrade’s blood debt.
He gave himself over to pure rage, without a thought for the cost.
And Song Ilseom wasn’t the only one who felt it.
“How dare you...!”
“You bastards are lower than this beggar!”
Sssshing! Slice!
Ju Hwaran, Gung Gibang, and the thousand defenders who had barely survived gritted their teeth and forced themselves to their feet.
Hope that they could win?
They’d long since erased it from their hearts.
The monsters had stopped moving, but fanatics remained—several times as many. Worse, tens of thousands of enemy reinforcements had appeared.
But hope wasn’t the only thing that could move people.
In that dark, bottomless despair, they had seen it clearly:
Hyuk Mujin, refusing to lose his dignity until the very last moment before he fell.
*Fire Dragon Pavilion... No.*
Before an enemy they could not possibly defeat, his spirit had not bent.
*Swift Wind Sword Hyuk Mujin.*
CLANG-CLANG-CLANG!
At last, a thousand blades began to shine again, rippling like a wave.
The defenders clamped their hands over severed arms and slashed-open bellies. They bit their tongues to suppress their pain and fear, gripped their weapons, and stood.
With all their strength, they shouted what might be their last words—the final proof that they had existed in this world.
“Knife-and-Dagger Hero So Gyuhyeok is here!”
“Swift Blade Shakes the Heavens Mu Cheol is here too!”
“Figures the orthodox faction would have such fancy titles. I’m Black-Killing Sword Jo Hyeok, you bastards!”
Masters of the orthodox faction, the unorthodox faction, and those who belonged somewhere between the two.
Their roots, their branches, and the fruit they bore were different. But the great cause they sought to protect was the same.
“Destroy the Demonic Path and restore Heaven.”
Destroy the Demonic Path and set the heavens right.

An old Daoist murmured the four characters they had once shouted until they were spitting blood, back when they fought a hundred thousand followers of the Demonic Path. He tightened his grip on his sword.
Slice.
A body split into dozens of pieces along a streak of white light and scattered.
The Black Ghost had finally met its true end. The old Daoist turned away, and Cheongheoja’s voice rang out, carrying the force of his internal energy.
“I miss those days. The time when you and I were ‘us.’ Don’t you?”
In Cheongheoja’s eyes, steeped in sorrow and anger, a huge figure stood before the ruined gate in the distance.
“Seafaring King Pa Ryun.”
The next moment—
“You haven’t changed, Cheongheoja.”
With a heavy voice that brushed over Hyuk Mujin’s fallen head, the master of the long, vast Yangtze strode out beneath the faint moonlight.
Two more unwelcome guests emerged from behind his imposing frame.
One was a mysterious figure dressed in black from head to toe. The other, a slight old man standing beside him, had a familiar face.
“It’s been a long time, Cheongheoja.”
At the greeting, Cheongheoja’s gaze turned cold.
“Right. You were there too. Green Forest Battle King Tae Gunak.”
“Such a sharp edge to your words. Last time we met, I believe you called me a fellow Daoist, not ‘you.’”
“Those days will never return. Not after the irrevocable choices some people made.”
Tae Gunak looked around, his brow furrowing slightly.
“I’m sorry things came to this. I mean that.”
“You mean that...”
Cheongheoja murmured the words hollowly, then drew up every last bit of his remaining internal energy.
Hummm.
As if sensing that his master’s end was near, the treasured sword that had been with him all his life trembled.
Not far away, Great Sir was still struggling against Black Ghost. But Cheongheoja’s senses and energy had already focused entirely on the unwelcome guests guarding the gate.
He had to bring down more than the two giants who divided the world’s dark-path forces between them.
There was also the mysterious man in black. Instinct told Cheongheoja he was no weaker than either of them.
*He must be one of Dark Heaven’s key figures. But who?*
The question crossed his mind, but Cheongheoja could only smile bitterly.
Worry was ultimately a luxury for those who survived.
For an old Daoist who had to face three Supreme Peak masters alone, there was no point in worrying any further.
All he could do was resolve to meet his end without shame before those remarkable young people, still advancing as they cut down their enemies.
“Come, you thieves of the world. I am Cheongheoja of Kunlun.”
The old Daoist’s eyes flashed, colder than ever.
“Let’s finish this quickly.”
A quiet voice reached every ear.
Rumble.
The black-robed man stepped forward, and immense qi began to churn around him.

Cheongheoja, charging with all his strength. Great Sir, fleeing in haste from the Black Ghost’s sword. The Fire Dragon Pavilion members fighting their way through the fanatics, and the thousand defenders following them in their final stand.
Every one of them stared wide-eyed, trembling at the eruption of power that filled their vision as though it would be the last thing they ever saw.
SHWAAAA!
A single line—impossible to block, impossible even to see clearly—cut across the world.
Why had his body suddenly gone rigid?
Where had this enormous rock come from, pressing down on his chest?
Jin Taekyung couldn’t tell what had caused it or why.
No—he didn’t want to know.
The moment he found out what this sudden feeling of dread meant, he felt the last thread barely holding him together might snap.
But despite that, Jin Taekyung’s gaze toward somewhere in the east, hidden behind enemies and buildings, had begun to tremble.
*This is...*
His vision was blurred as though by mist, his senses dull as an axe waiting for winter. His whole body sagged like waterlogged cotton.
Even so, he could faintly hear and feel it.
The enormous blast that had rung out far to the east. The steep surge of power.
It pointed to only one thing.
